subject: social-sciences-sp
description: Social Sciences Senior Phase (Grades 7–9) question bank. One 20-item pool per atomic skill (the topic key IS the skill id). Content subject: 0.6 pass mark, mastery via lib/content-mastery.ts.

SSSP.G7.H1.A1.title: Trade across the Sahara
SSSP.G7.H1.A1.description: History (CAPS G7 T1) — The kingdom of Mali & Timbuktu: Trade across the Sahara.
SSSP.G7.H1.A1.recovery_strategy: Picture the caravan route: salt comes south, gold goes north.

questions.question: Which animal carried goods across the Sahara Desert in the trans-Saharan trade?
questions.memo: Camels can travel long distances across the desert with little water, so traders moved goods in camel caravans.

questions.question: Salt was carried south across the Sahara and exchanged for gold.
questions.memo: Salt was scarce in West Africa but gold was plentiful, so salt moving south was swapped for gold moving north.

questions.question: Which of these was NOT a major good traded across the Sahara?
questions.memo: Sahara trade moved gold, salt, ivory, enslaved people and ostrich feathers — not tea from China.

questions.question: Islam spread into West Africa mainly through which group of people?
questions.memo: Muslim traders carried their religion along the caravan routes, so Islam spread into West Africa through trade.

questions.question: A group of camels and traders travelling together across the desert was called a ____.
questions.memo: A caravan is a group of traders and pack animals travelling together for safety across the desert.

questions.question: Trans-Saharan trade connected West Africa with North Africa and the Mediterranean.
questions.memo: Goods, ideas and religion flowed between West Africa and North Africa across the Sahara trade routes.

questions.question: Why was salt so valuable in West Africa?
options: It was scarce and needed to preserve food
It was used as money everywhere
It could only be mined in Europe
It was used to make weapons
questions.expected: It was scarce and needed to preserve food
questions.memo: Salt was rare in West Africa and essential for preserving food and health, which made it extremely valuable.

questions.question: Put these steps of a trans-Saharan trade journey in order.

items.text: Traders load salt onto camels in North Africa
The caravan crosses the Sahara Desert
Salt is exchanged for gold in West Africa
Gold is carried back north to the Mediterranean

questions.memo: Salt went south, was swapped for gold, and the gold travelled north — the heart of the trans-Saharan trade.

questions.question: Sort each item by the direction it usually travelled in the Sahara trade.

buckets.label: Carried NORTH out of West Africa

questions.expected: Salt and Mediterranean goods came south; gold and ivory went north.
questions.memo: West Africa sent out its gold and ivory, and received salt and manufactured goods from the north.

questions.question: The trans-Saharan trade helped which kind of settlement to grow in West Africa?
questions.memo: Trade brought wealth that allowed towns and cities like Timbuktu to grow into important centres.

questions.question: Camel caravans usually crossed the Sahara alone with a single trader.
questions.memo: Crossing the desert was dangerous, so traders travelled together in large caravans for safety.

questions.question: Roughly when did Islam begin spreading across North Africa into West Africa via traders?
questions.memo: From about the 9th century, Muslim traders spread Islam south along the caravan routes into West Africa.

questions.question: The Sahara is the world's largest hot ____.
questions.memo: The Sahara is the largest hot desert, which is why crossing it needed camels and caravans.

questions.question: Ostrich feathers were among the goods traded from West Africa.
questions.memo: Gold, ivory, enslaved people and ostrich feathers were traded out of West Africa.

questions.question: Trade goods from Europe and North Africa entered West Africa in exchange for gold and other goods. This makes the Sahara trade an example of:
questions.memo: Goods crossed the whole desert between regions — long-distance trade.

questions.question: Traders relied on oases — places in the desert with ____.
questions.memo: Oases provided water, vital rest stops on the desert crossing.

questions.question: Without camels, crossing the Sahara for trade would have been far harder.
questions.memo: Camels made the desert crossing possible, so they were central to the trade.

questions.question: The spread of Islam along the trade routes is an example of trade carrying:
options: Ideas and religion, not just goods
questions.expected: Ideas and religion, not just goods
questions.memo: Trade routes carried ideas and religion as well as goods.

questions.question: Which best describes a caravan route?
options: A regular path traders followed across the desert
questions.expected: A regular path traders followed across the desert
questions.memo: Caravan routes were the established paths traders used across the Sahara.

questions.question: Trade made some West African towns wealthy and important.
questions.memo: Trade wealth helped towns like Timbuktu grow rich and important.

questions.question: Why did traders value gold from West Africa so highly?
options: It was rare and beautiful and did not rust
questions.expected: It was rare and beautiful and did not rust
questions.memo: Gold's rarity and lasting shine made it highly valued.

questions.question: Goods moving in both directions made the Sahara a busy ____ route.
questions.memo: The Sahara was a busy two-way trade route.

questions.question: North Africa borders the Mediterranean Sea, linking Saharan trade to Europe.
questions.memo: Goods reached the Mediterranean and Europe through North Africa.

questions.question: A historian studying Saharan trade might use which source?
questions.memo: Written accounts by travellers are valuable historical sources.

SSSP.G7.H1.A2.title: The kingdom of Mali
SSSP.G7.H1.A2.description: History (CAPS G7 T1) — The kingdom of Mali & Timbuktu: The kingdom of Mali.
SSSP.G7.H1.A2.recovery_strategy: Mansa Musa = Mali's richest king, famous for his hajj to Mecca.

questions.question: Who was the famous ruler of Mali at the height of its power in the early 14th century?
questions.memo: Mansa Musa ruled Mali at its richest and most powerful, in the early 1300s.

questions.question: Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca.
questions.memo: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca was so rich that it became famous across the world.

questions.question: Mansa Musa's wealth came mainly from Mali's control of which resource?
questions.memo: Mali's power rested on its control of West African gold, which made its rulers extremely wealthy.

questions.question: A great ____ was built in the kingdom of Mali as a place of Muslim worship.
questions.memo: Mali's rulers were Muslim and built grand mosques, including the famous Great Mosque.

questions.question: Which religion did Mansa Musa follow?
questions.memo: Mansa Musa was a Muslim ruler, which is why he made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

questions.question: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage showed the world how wealthy the kingdom of Mali was.
questions.memo: He travelled with so much gold that his journey advertised Mali's enormous wealth to other lands.

questions.question: Where was Mecca, the destination of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage?
questions.memo: Mecca, the holiest city of Islam, is in Arabia — a very long journey from Mali.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the kingdom of Mali under Mansa Musa?
options: An empty desert with no people
questions.memo: Mali was a large, rich and well-run kingdom whose ruler was a devout Muslim.

questions.question: Mali was located in West Africa.
questions.memo: The kingdom of Mali lay in West Africa, controlling the gold and the trade routes of the region.

questions.question: Mansa Musa's journey to Mecca is known as a ____.
questions.memo: A pilgrimage is a religious journey to a holy place — for Muslims, the hajj to Mecca.

questions.question: Why is Mansa Musa often described as one of the richest people in history?
options: He controlled vast amounts of gold
questions.expected: He controlled vast amounts of gold
questions.memo: His control over West Africa's gold made him fabulously wealthy by any measure.

questions.question: Mali's rulers had no interest in religion or learning.
questions.memo: Mali's Muslim rulers supported religion and learning, funding mosques and centres of study.

questions.question: Mali grew wealthy mainly by controlling trade in gold and ____.
questions.memo: Mali controlled the trade in gold and salt, the two great Saharan goods.

questions.question: Mansa is a title meaning king or emperor.
questions.memo: 'Mansa' was the title of Mali's rulers, meaning king or emperor.

questions.question: Mansa Musa's journey passed through which famous Egyptian city on the way to Mecca?
questions.memo: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage passed through Cairo, where his spending became legendary.

questions.question: Mali was a powerful ____ in West Africa in the 14th century.
questions.memo: Mali was a powerful West African kingdom at its height in the 1300s.

questions.question: Mali's wealth allowed it to support learning and grand buildings.
questions.memo: Trade wealth funded mosques, learning and grand architecture in Mali.

questions.question: Mansa Musa is best remembered as a ruler who was:
options: Extremely wealthy and a devout Muslim
questions.expected: Extremely wealthy and a devout Muslim
questions.memo: He is remembered for his vast wealth and his Muslim faith.

questions.question: A pilgrimage to Mecca is one of the duties of which faith?
questions.memo: The hajj to Mecca is a duty for Muslims who are able to make it.

questions.question: Mali had no trade links with North Africa.
questions.memo: Mali traded heavily across the Sahara with North Africa.

questions.question: The Great Mosque built in Mali shows the kingdom's:
questions.memo: Building a great mosque displayed Mali's wealth and Islamic faith.

questions.question: Mansa Musa ruled in the early ____ century.
questions.memo: Mansa Musa ruled Mali at its height in the early 14th century (1300s).

questions.question: Mali's gold was important far beyond West Africa.
questions.memo: Mali's gold was valued across North Africa, the Mediterranean and beyond.

questions.question: Why do we know about Mansa Musa today?
options: His wealth and pilgrimage were widely recorded
questions.expected: His wealth and pilgrimage were widely recorded
questions.memo: Accounts of his famous pilgrimage spread his fame and preserved his story.

SSSP.G7.H1.A3.title: The city of Timbuktu
SSSP.G7.H1.A3.description: History (CAPS G7 T1) — The kingdom of Mali & Timbuktu: The city of Timbuktu.
SSSP.G7.H1.A3.recovery_strategy: Timbuktu was famous for two things: trade AND books/learning.

questions.question: Timbuktu was famous as a centre of both trade and ____.
questions.memo: Timbuktu was known for trade AND for learning — scholars studied many subjects there.

questions.question: Timbuktu lay on the trans-Saharan caravan route.
questions.memo: Timbuktu's position on the caravan route made it a busy meeting point for traders.

questions.question: Which traveller wrote descriptions of Timbuktu in his book 'Description of Africa' (1550)?
questions.memo: Leo Africanus described his travels to Timbuktu in his famous 1550 book.

questions.question: At Timbuktu, salt brought across the desert was traded mainly for what?
questions.memo: Like the wider Sahara trade, salt arriving in Timbuktu was exchanged for gold.

questions.question: Which subjects were studied by scholars in Timbuktu?
questions.memo: Timbuktu's scholars studied mathematics, astronomy, medicine, law, history and more.

questions.question: The Timbuktu manuscripts are old handwritten books that record the city's learning.
questions.memo: The manuscripts are precious handwritten records of the scholarship of Timbuktu, now being preserved.

questions.question: Why is Timbuktu recognised as a World Heritage Site today?
options: Its great history of trade and learning
questions.expected: Its great history of trade and learning
questions.memo: Timbuktu is a World Heritage Site because of its outstanding history as a centre of trade and learning.

questions.question: Old handwritten books preserved in Timbuktu are called ____.
questions.memo: Manuscripts are handwritten documents — Timbuktu's are a treasured record of African scholarship.

questions.question: South African scholars have helped to preserve the Timbuktu manuscripts.
questions.memo: South Africa collaborated on a project to help conserve and study the Timbuktu manuscripts.

questions.question: Which two things made Timbuktu important?
questions.memo: Remember Timbuktu for two things together: it was a trade centre and a centre of learning.

questions.question: In this description, tap the phrases that show Timbuktu was a centre of LEARNING.
questions.source_text: Timbuktu stood on the caravan route where salt was traded for gold. Its scholars studied mathematics and astronomy, and its libraries held thousands of manuscripts.
questions.task: Select the phrases about learning (not trade).

targets.reason: Libraries and manuscripts show a centre of learning.

questions.memo: The scholars, libraries and manuscripts all point to learning; the salt-for-gold line is about trade.

questions.question: Timbuktu was a poor, unknown village with no contact with other places.
questions.memo: Timbuktu was a famous, wealthy and connected city known across the Muslim world for trade and learning.

questions.question: Timbuktu is located near which great African river?
questions.memo: Timbuktu lies near the Niger River, aiding its trade.

questions.question: Timbuktu had famous centres of Islamic learning.
questions.memo: Timbuktu's mosques and schools were renowned centres of Islamic learning.

questions.question: Manuscripts are valuable to historians because they:
questions.memo: Manuscripts preserve past knowledge, making them precious historical sources.

questions.question: Timbuktu attracted students and ____ from far away.
questions.memo: Scholars travelled to Timbuktu to study and teach.

questions.question: Salt and gold were both traded at Timbuktu.
questions.memo: Timbuktu was a market where salt was exchanged for gold.

questions.question: Being a World Heritage Site means Timbuktu is recognised as:
questions.memo: World Heritage status marks a place of outstanding value to all humanity.

questions.question: The Timbuktu manuscripts deal with subjects such as:
questions.memo: The manuscripts cover astronomy, medicine, law, history and more.

questions.question: Preserving the manuscripts protects African history and knowledge.
questions.memo: Conserving the manuscripts safeguards a record of African scholarship.

questions.question: Timbuktu's importance shows that Africa had:
options: Centres of learning and trade long ago
questions.expected: Centres of learning and trade long ago
questions.memo: Timbuktu proves Africa had advanced centres of trade and learning long ago.

questions.question: Timbuktu sat on a major ____ route across the Sahara.
questions.memo: Timbuktu was a key stop on the trans-Saharan caravan route.

questions.question: Leo Africanus visited Timbuktu and wrote about it.
questions.memo: Leo Africanus described Timbuktu after visiting it, in his 1550 book.

questions.question: Why is it important to study places like Timbuktu?
options: They challenge the false idea that Africa had no rich history
questions.expected: They challenge the false idea that Africa had no rich history
questions.memo: Timbuktu reminds us of Africa's rich past of learning and trade.

SSSP.G7.H2.A1.title: West Africa & slavery before Europeans
SSSP.G7.H2.A1.description: History (CAPS G7 T2) — The Transatlantic slave trade: West Africa & slavery before Europeans.
SSSP.G7.H2.A1.recovery_strategy: Slavery existed before Europeans, but the Atlantic trade was far larger and harsher.

questions.question: Did slavery exist in West Africa before Europeans arrived?
options: Yes, but it was different from Atlantic slavery
questions.expected: Yes, but it was different from Atlantic slavery
questions.memo: Forms of slavery existed in West Africa before Europeans, but the Atlantic trade was far larger and more brutal.

questions.question: The transatlantic slave trade was much larger than slavery that existed in West Africa before Europeans.
questions.memo: The Atlantic trade forcibly moved millions of people — far more than earlier West African slavery.

questions.question: Before the European slave trade, West Africa was home to what?
questions.memo: West Africa had well-organised societies, kingdoms and busy trade long before Europeans arrived.

questions.question: West Africa had no contact with trade before Europeans came.
questions.memo: West Africa already had rich trade networks, including the trans-Saharan trade, before the Atlantic trade.

questions.question: How was slavery in West Africa generally different from later Atlantic slavery?
options: Enslaved people could sometimes keep rights or status
It moved people across the ocean
questions.expected: Enslaved people could sometimes keep rights or status
questions.memo: In some West African societies enslaved people kept certain rights — unlike the harsh, permanent plantation slavery of the Americas.

questions.question: West Africa was organised into ____ and societies with their own rulers and trade.
questions.memo: West Africa had kingdoms with their own rulers, trade and culture before European contact.

questions.question: Which earlier trade route already linked West Africa to the wider world?
questions.memo: The trans-Saharan trade had long connected West Africa northwards across the desert.

questions.question: The arrival of Europeans changed the scale and nature of slavery in West Africa dramatically.
questions.memo: European demand for plantation labour turned slavery into a vast, brutal trade across the Atlantic.

questions.question: West African kingdoms before Europeans were often organised around:
questions.memo: These societies had rulers, farming and busy trade long before Europeans.

questions.question: The Atlantic slave trade forced far more people across the ocean than earlier West African slavery moved.
questions.memo: The Atlantic trade was vastly larger in scale than earlier West African slavery.

questions.question: Why is it important to know West Africa had organised societies before Europeans?
options: It corrects the false idea that Africa had no history
questions.expected: It corrects the false idea that Africa had no history
questions.memo: Knowing this corrects the myth that Africa lacked its own rich history.

questions.question: Before the Atlantic trade, West Africa traded across the ____ Desert.
questions.memo: West Africa was already linked to the world by trans-Saharan trade.

questions.question: All forms of slavery are exactly the same.
questions.memo: Slavery took different forms; Atlantic plantation slavery was uniquely vast and brutal.

questions.question: Comparing slavery before and after Europeans is an example of which history skill?
questions.memo: Comparing the two is using the skill of change and continuity over time.

questions.question: West African societies had their own:
questions.memo: They had rich languages, cultures and trade of their own.

questions.question: European demand for plantation labour greatly increased the scale of slavery.
questions.memo: Europe's plantation economy drove the huge expansion of the Atlantic slave trade.

questions.question: A 'kingdom' is a society ruled by a:
questions.memo: A kingdom is ruled by a king or queen — West Africa had several.

questions.question: The Atlantic slave trade moved people across the ____ Ocean.
questions.memo: The trade carried people across the Atlantic to the Americas.

questions.question: Trade in West Africa existed only after Europeans arrived.
questions.memo: West Africa had thriving trade long before Europeans came.

questions.question: Studying West Africa before the slave trade helps us understand:
options: What was lost and changed by the trade
questions.expected: What was lost and changed by the trade
questions.memo: It shows what these societies were like before the trade disrupted them.

SSSP.G7.H2.A2.title: Slavery in the American South
SSSP.G7.H2.A2.description: History (CAPS G7 T2) — The Transatlantic slave trade: Slavery in the American South.
SSSP.G7.H2.A2.recovery_strategy: Follow the chain: captured in West Africa → Middle Passage → sold → plantation.

questions.question: Enslaved people in the American South were forced to work mainly on what?
questions.memo: Most enslaved people in the American South worked on large farms called plantations.

questions.question: Which of these was a major plantation crop in the American South?
questions.memo: Cotton, rice, sugar cane and tobacco were all grown on plantations using enslaved labour.

questions.question: The terrible sea voyage that carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic was called the ____ Passage.
questions.memo: The Middle Passage was the brutal Atlantic crossing in which many enslaved people died.

questions.question: Plantation owners used enslaved labour because it was cheap and they did not have to pay wages.
questions.memo: Enslaved people were not paid, so plantation owners used their forced labour to make large profits.

questions.question: Put the stages of the transatlantic slave trade in the correct order.

items.text: People are captured in West Africa
They are sold to European traders on the coast
They cross the Atlantic on the Middle Passage
They are sold and forced to work on plantations

questions.memo: Capture → sale on the coast → Middle Passage → plantation labour: the path of the Atlantic slave trade.

questions.question: Where were enslaved people captured before being shipped across the Atlantic?
questions.memo: Enslaved people were captured in West Africa and transported across the Atlantic to the Americas.

questions.question: Conditions on the Middle Passage were comfortable for the enslaved people.
questions.memo: The Middle Passage was overcrowded, cruel and deadly — conditions were horrific.

questions.question: Raw materials like cotton produced by enslaved people were mostly sent to be made into goods where?
questions.memo: Plantation raw materials such as cotton fed Britain's factories, linking slavery to the Industrial Revolution.

questions.question: A place where enslaved people were bought and sold was called a slave ____.
questions.memo: Enslaved people were treated as property and sold at slave markets.

questions.question: Millions of enslaved Africans were taken across the Atlantic to the Americas.
questions.memo: Over the centuries of the trade, millions of Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic.

questions.question: Why did plantation owners want a large number of enslaved workers?
options: Growing crops like cotton and sugar needed heavy labour
questions.expected: Growing crops like cotton and sugar needed heavy labour
questions.memo: Plantation crops needed huge amounts of hard labour, which owners forced enslaved people to provide.

questions.question: Tobacco, rice and sugar cane were grown on:
questions.memo: These cash crops were grown on plantations with enslaved labour.

questions.question: Enslaved people were treated as property to be bought and sold.
questions.memo: Under slavery, people were owned as property and sold at markets.

questions.question: Cotton from the American South was important to industry in:
questions.memo: Southern cotton fed British textile factories.

questions.question: The forced ocean voyage of enslaved Africans was the Middle ____.
questions.memo: The Middle Passage was the brutal Atlantic crossing.

questions.question: Many enslaved people died during the Middle Passage.
questions.memo: Overcrowding, disease and cruelty killed many during the crossing.

questions.question: Why did plantation owners want enslaved labour rather than paid workers?
options: To increase profit by not paying wages
questions.expected: To increase profit by not paying wages
questions.memo: Forced, unpaid labour increased plantation profits.

questions.question: Raw materials from plantations were turned into goods in:
questions.memo: Plantation raw materials were processed in factories, often in Britain.

questions.question: The slave trade linked Africa, the Americas and Europe.
questions.memo: The Atlantic trade connected three continents in a system of forced labour and goods.

questions.question: A plantation was a:
options: Large farm growing one main crop
questions.expected: Large farm growing one main crop
questions.memo: Plantations were large farms focused on a single cash crop.

questions.question: Enslaved people were sold at a slave ____.
questions.memo: Enslaved people were bought and sold at slave markets.

questions.question: Slavery in the American South was gentle and fair.
questions.memo: Plantation slavery was harsh, cruel and based on force.

questions.question: The huge profits from plantation crops mainly benefited:
options: Owners, and economies in America and Britain
questions.expected: Owners, and economies in America and Britain
questions.memo: Profits flowed to owners and to the American and British economies.

SSSP.G7.H2.A3.title: Impact on enslaved people
SSSP.G7.H2.A3.description: History (CAPS G7 T2) — The Transatlantic slave trade: Impact on enslaved people.
SSSP.G7.H2.A3.recovery_strategy: Resistance ranged from quiet (go-slow) to open revolt and escape.

questions.question: Which of these was a way enslaved people quietly resisted slavery?
questions.memo: Quiet (passive) resistance included working slowly, breaking tools and pretending not to understand.

questions.question: Who was the enslaved woman who escaped and then helped many others reach freedom?
questions.memo: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and guided many others to freedom via the Underground Railroad.

questions.question: What was the Underground Railroad?
options: A secret network of routes and safe houses for escaping slaves
questions.expected: A secret network of routes and safe houses for escaping slaves
questions.memo: The Underground Railroad was a secret network helping enslaved people escape to free areas.

questions.question: Nat Turner led a slave revolt in 1831.
questions.memo: Nat Turner's revolt of 1831 was a famous armed uprising against slavery.

questions.question: The Amistad mutiny of 1839 was led by which captured African?
questions.memo: Joseph Cinque led the famous rebellion aboard the slave ship Amistad in 1839.

questions.question: Sort each act of resistance as passive (quiet) or active (open).
questions.expected: Slow work and breaking tools are passive; rebellion and escape are active.
questions.memo: Resistance ranged from quiet sabotage (passive) to open revolt and escape (active).

questions.question: Enslaved people kept their culture alive through songs and stories.
questions.memo: Songs, stories and faith helped enslaved communities keep their culture and hope alive.

questions.question: John Brown is remembered for his mission to do what?
questions.memo: John Brown fought to abolish slavery, even leading an armed raid for the cause.

questions.question: Running away from a plantation to escape slavery is an example of ____ resistance.
questions.memo: Escaping was a bold, active form of resistance against slavery.

questions.question: Why did enslaved people resist in many different ways rather than one way?
options: Open rebellion was dangerous, so they also used safer quiet methods
They were not allowed to rebel openly only on Sundays
They had no reason to resist
questions.expected: Open rebellion was dangerous, so they also used safer quiet methods
questions.memo: Open revolt risked death, so resistance ranged from quiet sabotage to escape to rebellion.

questions.question: Resistance to slavery only ever took the form of large armed revolts.
questions.memo: Most resistance was quieter — go-slows, sabotage, escape — alongside the rarer armed revolts.

questions.question: Spirituals and work songs were part of enslaved people's:
questions.memo: Songs and stories helped enslaved communities endure and keep their culture.

questions.question: The Underground Railroad used safe houses to help escapees.
questions.memo: Safe houses and secret routes formed the Underground Railroad.

questions.question: Harriet Tubman is admired because she:
options: Escaped and returned to free others
questions.expected: Escaped and returned to free others
questions.memo: After escaping, Tubman risked her life to free many others.

questions.question: Nat Turner led a slave ____ in 1831.
questions.memo: Nat Turner's 1831 revolt was an armed uprising against slavery.

questions.question: Resisting slavery could be very dangerous.
questions.memo: Resistance risked brutal punishment or death, so many forms were secret.

questions.question: Pretending to be sick to avoid work was a form of:
questions.memo: Feigning illness was a subtle, passive form of resistance.

questions.question: The story of the Amistad involves enslaved people who:
questions.memo: The Amistad captives rebelled aboard the slave ship in 1839.

questions.question: Some white people, like John Brown, also fought against slavery.
questions.memo: Abolitionists such as John Brown fought to end slavery.

questions.question: Keeping their own stories and beliefs helped enslaved people to:
questions.memo: Culture and faith helped enslaved people keep their identity and hope.

questions.question: Helping enslaved people escape to free areas was the work of the Underground ____.
questions.memo: The Underground Railroad helped people escape to freedom.

questions.question: Escaping slavery was easy and safe.
questions.memo: Escape was extremely dangerous, with severe punishment if caught.

questions.question: Studying resistance shows that enslaved people:
options: Actively fought their conditions in many ways
questions.expected: Actively fought their conditions in many ways
questions.memo: Resistance proves enslaved people constantly struggled against their bondage.

SSSP.G7.H2.A4.title: Impact on economies
SSSP.G7.H2.A4.description: History (CAPS G7 T2) — The Transatlantic slave trade: Impact on economies.
SSSP.G7.H2.A4.recovery_strategy: One side grew rich; the other lost people and wealth.

questions.question: Which regions gained great wealth from the transatlantic slave trade?
questions.memo: America and Britain profited enormously, while West Africa suffered lasting harm.

questions.question: The slave trade caused lasting harm to West Africa.
questions.memo: West Africa lost millions of people and suffered deep, lasting economic and social damage.

questions.question: How did the slave trade help Britain's economy?
options: Profits and raw materials helped fund its growth and factories
It gave Britain gold mines in Africa
It had no effect at all
questions.expected: Profits and raw materials helped fund its growth and factories
questions.memo: Slave-trade profits and plantation raw materials fed Britain's growing economy and industry.

questions.question: What did West Africa lose because of the slave trade?
options: Millions of young people and stability
questions.expected: Millions of young people and stability
questions.memo: Losing millions of mostly young people robbed West Africa of workers, families and stability.

questions.question: The slave trade brought wealth to Britain and America but ____ to West Africa.
questions.memo: One side grew rich while the other suffered lasting damage — an unequal and unjust exchange.

questions.question: The slave trade affected the economies of three regions: West Africa, America and Britain.
questions.memo: The trade tied together West Africa, the Americas and Britain in an Atlantic economy built on enslaved labour.

questions.question: Sort each outcome by who experienced it from the slave trade.

items.text: Loss of millions of young people

questions.expected: Britain and America gained profits and materials; West Africa lost people and stability.
questions.memo: The trade enriched Britain and America while devastating West Africa.

questions.question: Why is the transatlantic slave trade described as 'unequal' in its effects?
options: It enriched some regions while devastating another
questions.expected: It enriched some regions while devastating another
questions.memo: The benefits and the suffering fell on different regions, making the trade deeply unequal.

questions.question: The slave trade is part of why some economies grew rich while others were:
questions.memo: It enriched some while damaging West Africa — an unequal outcome.

questions.question: Profits from slavery helped fund Britain's growth.
questions.memo: Slave-trade and plantation profits helped finance Britain's economic growth.

questions.question: Losing millions of young people harmed West Africa's:
questions.memo: Losing so many young people robbed West Africa of workers and weakened societies.

questions.question: The slave trade had ____ effects on different regions.
questions.memo: Its effects were deeply unequal — wealth for some, devastation for others.

questions.question: The transatlantic slave trade affected three continents.
questions.memo: Africa, the Americas and Europe were all tied into the trade.

questions.question: Cheap raw materials from plantations helped power which revolution in Britain?
questions.memo: Plantation raw materials helped fuel Britain's Industrial Revolution.

questions.question: Why do historians call the slave trade's effects on West Africa long-lasting?
questions.memo: The damage to West African societies lasted for generations.

questions.question: Britain and America were the regions that gained most economically.
questions.memo: Britain and America gained the most wealth from the trade.

questions.question: The slave trade shows how economic gain can be built on:
questions.memo: The wealth created rested on the suffering of enslaved people.

questions.question: West Africa suffered lasting ____ from the slave trade.
questions.memo: West Africa suffered deep, lasting damage.

questions.question: Everyone involved in the slave trade benefited equally.
questions.memo: The benefits and the suffering fell on different regions — it was deeply unequal.

questions.question: Understanding the economic effects helps us see that history shapes:
questions.memo: Historic injustices like the slave trade still shape inequalities today.

SSSP.G7.H3.A1.title: Indigenous peoples of the Cape
SSSP.G7.H3.A1.description: History (CAPS G7 T3) — Colonisation of the Cape (17th–18th C): Indigenous peoples of the Cape.
SSSP.G7.H3.A1.recovery_strategy: Khoikhoi = herders, San = hunter-gatherers, African farmers = further east.

questions.question: Which people were herders living at the Cape when the Dutch arrived?
questions.memo: The Khoikhoi were herders living at the Cape long before the Dutch arrived in 1652.

questions.question: The San people of the Cape mainly lived as what?
questions.memo: The San were hunter-gatherers, living by hunting animals and gathering plants.

questions.question: African farmers were settled to the east of the Cape, in the summer-rainfall areas.
questions.memo: African farmers settled in the wetter summer-rainfall areas to the east, suited to their crops.

questions.question: Why did African farmers settle to the east rather than at the Cape itself?
options: Their crops (sorghum, millet) needed summer rainfall
There was gold in the east
questions.expected: Their crops (sorghum, millet) needed summer rainfall
questions.memo: Crops like sorghum and millet needed summer rain, so farmers settled in the eastern summer-rainfall zone.

questions.question: The ____ were herders, while the San were hunter-gatherers at the Cape.
questions.memo: Khoikhoi = herders; San = hunter-gatherers. Both lived at the Cape before colonisation.

questions.question: The Cape was empty of people before the Dutch arrived.
questions.memo: The Khoikhoi, San and (to the east) African farmers already lived in the region.

questions.question: Match each group to how they lived. Sort them into the correct way of life.
questions.expected: Khoikhoi = herders, San = hunter-gatherers, African farmers = crop farmers.
questions.memo: Three ways of life met around the Cape: herding, hunting-gathering and crop farming.

questions.question: In which century did the Dutch arrive to settle at the Cape?
questions.memo: The Dutch established their station at the Cape in 1652, in the 17th century.

questions.question: The Khoikhoi kept herds of:
questions.memo: The Khoikhoi were herders of cattle and sheep.

questions.question: The San lived by hunting wild animals and gathering plants.
questions.memo: The San were hunter-gatherers, living off wild animals and plants.

questions.question: African farmers settled to the east of the Cape because the area had:
questions.memo: Their crops needed summer rain, found in the eastern regions.

questions.question: Sorghum and ____ were crops grown by African farmers.
questions.memo: Sorghum and millet were staple crops needing summer rainfall.

questions.question: The Cape had several different groups of people before 1652.
questions.memo: Khoikhoi, San and (to the east) African farmers all lived in the region.

questions.question: Hunter-gatherers usually moved around because they:
questions.memo: The San moved to follow game and seasonal food sources.

questions.question: Herders like the Khoikhoi moved to find:
options: Grazing and water for their animals
questions.expected: Grazing and water for their animals
questions.memo: Herders moved to fresh grazing and water for their herds.

questions.question: The San left rock art that tells us about their lives.
questions.memo: San rock paintings are an important source about their culture and beliefs.

questions.question: Knowing about these groups corrects the false idea that the Cape was:
questions.memo: The land was already home to several peoples, not empty.

questions.question: The Khoikhoi were ____, while the San were hunter-gatherers.
questions.memo: Khoikhoi herders and San hunter-gatherers lived at the Cape.

questions.question: Climate affected where different groups could live and farm.
questions.memo: Rainfall and climate shaped where farming and herding were possible.

questions.question: Rock art is an example of a historical:
questions.memo: Rock art is a primary source telling us about San life.

SSSP.G7.H3.A2.title: Dutch settlement and the VOC
SSSP.G7.H3.A2.description: History (CAPS G7 T3) — Colonisation of the Cape (17th–18th C): Dutch settlement and the VOC.
SSSP.G7.H3.A2.recovery_strategy: The VOC came for a supply stop on the way to the East, not to farm.

questions.question: Which company set up a station at the Cape in 1652?
questions.memo: The VOC (Dutch East India Company) set up the Cape station in 1652.

questions.question: Why did the VOC want a station at the Cape?
options: As a refreshment stop for ships sailing to the East
questions.expected: As a refreshment stop for ships sailing to the East
questions.memo: The Cape was a halfway refreshment station supplying VOC ships on the long route to the East.

questions.question: The VOC first came to the Cape mainly to grow rich farms, not to supply ships.
questions.memo: The VOC's first aim was a supply stop for passing ships, not large-scale farming.

questions.question: Free burghers were what?
options: Former VOC employees allowed to farm for themselves
questions.expected: Former VOC employees allowed to farm for themselves
questions.memo: Free burghers were ex-Company servants released to farm and sell produce to the VOC.

questions.question: The French Huguenots who came to the Cape were known for which skill?
questions.memo: French Huguenot immigrants added farming and wine-making skills at the Cape.

questions.question: The ____ set up the Cape station in 1652 as a refreshment stop on the route to the East.
questions.memo: The VOC (Dutch East India Company) founded the Cape station in 1652.

questions.question: The Huguenots were religious refugees from France.
questions.memo: The Huguenots were French Protestants who fled religious persecution, some settling at the Cape.

questions.question: What did 'free burghers' do that the VOC depended on?
options: Produced food to supply the Company and its ships
questions.expected: Produced food to supply the Company and its ships
questions.memo: Free burghers farmed to supply food to the VOC and passing ships.

questions.question: The year 1652 is important because it marks the start of what at the Cape?
questions.memo: 1652 marks the start of permanent Dutch settlement at the Cape.

questions.question: The VOC was a powerful trading company from which country?
questions.memo: The VOC was the Dutch East India Company, from the Netherlands.

questions.question: The Cape station supplied fresh food and water to passing ships.
questions.memo: The station provided fresh supplies to VOC ships on the long voyage to the East.

questions.question: Jan van Riebeeck led the first VOC settlement at the Cape in:
questions.memo: Van Riebeeck established the VOC station in 1652.

questions.question: Former Company workers allowed to farm were called free ____.
questions.memo: Free burghers were ex-VOC servants released to farm.

questions.question: The Huguenots brought skills in farming and wine-making.
questions.memo: French Huguenot settlers added farming and wine-making skills.

questions.question: The Cape was useful to the VOC because it lay on the route between Europe and:
questions.memo: The Cape was a halfway stop on the Europe-to-Asia sea route.

questions.question: As free burghers farmed and expanded, they increasingly needed:
questions.memo: Farming expansion drove demand for land and labour, including enslaved people.

questions.question: The Huguenots were fleeing religious persecution in France.
questions.memo: Huguenots were Protestants who fled persecution in Catholic France.

questions.question: The VOC's main interest was:
questions.memo: The VOC was a trading company focused on profit.

questions.question: The year ____ marks the start of permanent European settlement at the Cape.
questions.memo: 1652 began permanent Dutch settlement at the Cape.

questions.question: The arrival of the VOC had no effect on the Khoikhoi.
questions.memo: VOC settlement increasingly took Khoikhoi land and disrupted their lives.

questions.question: Free burghers selling produce to the VOC shows the settlement was becoming:
options: A farming colony, not just a supply stop
questions.expected: A farming colony, not just a supply stop
questions.memo: Over time the Cape grew from a supply stop into a settled farming colony.

SSSP.G7.H3.A3.title: Slavery at the Cape
SSSP.G7.H3.A3.description: History (CAPS G7 T3) — Colonisation of the Cape (17th–18th C): Slavery at the Cape.
SSSP.G7.H3.A3.recovery_strategy: Cape slaves came mostly from the East and Africa — not the Atlantic trade.

questions.question: Why were enslaved people brought to the Cape?
options: To provide labour for the settlement and farms
questions.expected: To provide labour for the settlement and farms
questions.memo: The VOC and free burghers brought enslaved people to do the labour of the settlement and farms.

questions.question: Where did most enslaved people at the Cape come from?
options: East Africa, Madagascar and parts of Asia
questions.expected: East Africa, Madagascar and parts of Asia
questions.memo: Cape slaves came mostly from East Africa, Madagascar and Asia — not the Atlantic trade.

questions.question: Slavery at the Cape was the same as the transatlantic slave trade to America.
questions.memo: Cape slavery drew from the Indian Ocean world, not the Atlantic plantation system — a different system.

questions.question: Which religion was spread at the Cape partly through enslaved people from Asia?
questions.memo: Many enslaved people from Asia were Muslim, and Islam became part of the Cape's heritage.

questions.question: The development of which language was shaped partly by enslaved people at the Cape?
questions.memo: Enslaved people contributed to the development of the Afrikaans language at the Cape.

questions.question: Enslaved people at the Cape sometimes resisted their conditions.
questions.memo: Despite harsh control, enslaved people at the Cape resisted in various ways, met with severe punishment.

questions.question: Enslaved people brought to the Cape helped shape the religion of ____ and the Afrikaans language.
questions.memo: The legacy of Cape slavery includes Islam and contributions to Afrikaans.

questions.question: What is one lasting legacy of slavery at the Cape?
options: Cultural and religious heritage, including Islam
questions.expected: Cultural and religious heritage, including Islam
questions.memo: Cape slavery left a deep cultural and religious legacy, including Islam and influences on Afrikaans.

questions.question: Enslaved people had freedom to leave the Cape whenever they wished.
questions.memo: Enslaved people were owned and controlled, with no freedom to leave — that is what slavery meant.

questions.question: Enslaved people at the Cape were brought to do:
questions.memo: They were forced to do the hard labour of farms and homes.

questions.question: Cape slaves came mainly from the Atlantic plantation trade.
questions.memo: Cape slaves came largely from the Indian Ocean world (East Africa, Madagascar, Asia).

questions.question: The Afrikaans language was influenced by:
options: Enslaved people and many cultures at the Cape
questions.expected: Enslaved people and many cultures at the Cape
questions.memo: Afrikaans developed from the mixing of Dutch with the languages of enslaved and local people.

questions.question: Many enslaved people brought ____ to the Cape, now part of its heritage.
questions.memo: Islam, brought by enslaved people from Asia, became part of Cape heritage.

questions.question: Slave resistance at the Cape was punished harshly.
questions.memo: Resistance was met with severe punishment under the slave system.

questions.question: Enslaved people at the Cape had:
questions.memo: Enslaved people were owned and had no freedom or rights.

questions.question: The legacy of Cape slavery includes:
questions.memo: Cape slavery shaped religion (Islam), language (Afrikaans) and culture.

questions.question: Slavery shaped the society and culture of the Cape deeply.
questions.memo: Slavery left deep marks on Cape society, culture, religion and language.

questions.question: Where enslaved people came from shows the Cape was linked to:
questions.memo: Cape slavery connected it to East Africa, Madagascar and Asia.

questions.question: Enslaved people had no ____ to leave or choose their work.
questions.memo: Lack of freedom was the central reality of slavery.

questions.question: The story of enslaved people is an important part of South African history.
questions.memo: The history of slavery is a vital part of understanding South Africa.

questions.question: Studying slavery at the Cape helps us understand:
options: The roots of inequality and culture in South Africa
questions.expected: The roots of inequality and culture in South Africa
questions.memo: Cape slavery helps explain later inequality and the country's mixed culture.

SSSP.G7.H3.A4.title: Expanding frontiers and dispossession
SSSP.G7.H3.A4.description: History (CAPS G7 T3) — Colonisation of the Cape (17th–18th C): Expanding frontiers and dispossession.
SSSP.G7.H3.A4.recovery_strategy: As settlers moved inland, indigenous people lost land and independence.

questions.question: Who were the trekboers?
options: Dutch settlers who moved inland as roaming farmers
questions.expected: Dutch settlers who moved inland as roaming farmers
questions.memo: Trekboers were Dutch settler farmers who moved inland with their livestock, slaves and servants.

questions.question: As settlers moved inland, indigenous people lost land and independence.
questions.memo: The expanding frontier dispossessed the Khoikhoi and San of land and freedom.

questions.question: Genadendal (founded 1738) was the first what in southern Africa?
questions.memo: Genadendal, founded in 1738, was the first mission station in southern Africa.

questions.question: What happened to the Khoikhoi as the trekboers expanded?
options: They were dispossessed and many became servants
questions.expected: They were dispossessed and many became servants
questions.memo: Losing their land, many Khoikhoi were forced into service for the trekboers.

questions.question: Roaming Dutch settler farmers who moved inland with their livestock were called ____.
questions.memo: Trekboers were the mobile settler farmers of the expanding Cape frontier.

questions.question: The expansion of the Cape frontier had no effect on the people already living there.
questions.memo: The frontier's expansion dispossessed indigenous people of land and independence — a major effect.

questions.question: A mission station like Genadendal was set up mainly to do what?
options: Spread Christianity and offer a settled community
questions.expected: Spread Christianity and offer a settled community
questions.memo: Mission stations spread Christianity and provided settled communities, sometimes for dispossessed people.

questions.question: William Bleek and Lucy Lloyd are remembered for recording what?
questions.memo: Bleek and Lloyd recorded San language and folklore, preserving a precious record of San culture.

questions.question: Land dispossession was a major consequence of the expanding Cape frontier.
questions.memo: Indigenous people losing their land — dispossession — was a central consequence of frontier expansion.

questions.question: Trekboers were always on the move because they:
questions.memo: Trekboers moved inland constantly to find grazing for their livestock.

questions.question: As trekboers expanded, the Khoikhoi lost grazing land and independence.
questions.memo: The frontier's spread dispossessed the Khoikhoi of land and freedom.

questions.question: A mission station aimed mainly to:
questions.memo: Mission stations spread Christianity and offered settled communities.

questions.question: Genadendal (1738) was the first ____ station in southern Africa.
questions.memo: Genadendal was the first mission station in southern Africa.

questions.question: Dispossession means people being deprived of their land.
questions.memo: Dispossession is the loss of land — central to the frontier story.

questions.question: Bleek and Lloyd helped preserve which culture's stories?
questions.memo: Bleek and Lloyd recorded San language and folklore.

questions.question: Losing their land forced many Khoikhoi to become:
questions.memo: Dispossessed Khoikhoi often had to work as servants for trekboers.

questions.question: The frontier was a place where different groups met, traded and clashed.
questions.memo: Frontiers were zones of contact — trade, mixing and conflict.

questions.question: The expansion of settlement is an example of a long-term:
questions.memo: Expanding settlement created long-term conflict over land.

questions.question: Trekboers moved with their livestock, slaves and ____.
questions.memo: Trekboers travelled with their livestock, enslaved people and servants.

questions.question: The work of Bleek and Lloyd is a valuable record of San heritage.
questions.memo: Their records preserve precious San language and stories.

questions.question: Dispossession of land had consequences that:
questions.memo: Land dispossession had deep, long-lasting consequences.

SSSP.G7.H4.A1.title: British arrival and expanding settlement
SSSP.G7.H4.A1.description: History (CAPS G7 T4) — Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C): British arrival and expanding settlement.
SSSP.G7.H4.A1.caps_topic: Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C)
SSSP.G7.H4.A1.recovery_strategy: Power shifted from the Dutch VOC to Britain.

questions.question: In the early 19th century, which power took control of the Cape from the Dutch?
questions.memo: Britain took over the Cape, so power shifted from the Dutch VOC to the British.

questions.question: British control led to more European settlement at the Cape in the early 1800s.
questions.memo: Under Britain, European settlement expanded, including the 1820 settlers.

questions.question: In the early 1800s the ____ took over the Cape Colony from the Dutch.
questions.memo: The British takeover marked a new colonial power at the Cape.

questions.question: The arrival of the British meant the frontier of European settlement did what?
questions.memo: Under British rule, European settlement and its frontier pushed further outward.

questions.question: Power at the Cape shifted from the Dutch VOC to Britain in the early 19th century.
questions.memo: The early 1800s saw the Cape pass from Dutch VOC control to the British Empire.

questions.question: More European settlers arriving usually increased what on the frontier?
questions.memo: More settlers meant more pressure and competition for land, fuelling frontier conflict.

questions.question: The 1820 Settlers were immigrants from:
questions.memo: The 1820 Settlers were British immigrants brought to the eastern Cape.

questions.question: British rule brought English language and laws to the Cape.
questions.memo: Under Britain, English language and British laws spread at the Cape.

questions.question: More settlers on the frontier increased pressure on:
questions.memo: More settlers meant more pressure on indigenous land, fuelling conflict.

questions.question: Britain took the Cape from the ____ in the early 1800s.
questions.memo: Britain took control of the Cape from the Dutch.

questions.question: The British placed 1820 settlers near the eastern frontier as a buffer.
questions.memo: The 1820 Settlers were placed on the eastern frontier partly as a buffer zone.

questions.question: A 'frontier' is best described as:
options: A border zone where groups meet
questions.expected: A border zone where groups meet
questions.memo: A frontier is the edge zone where different groups meet and often clash.

questions.question: British control of the Cape was part of Britain's growing:
questions.memo: The Cape became part of the expanding British Empire.

questions.question: Power at the Cape moved from the Dutch to the British.
questions.memo: Control of the Cape shifted from the Dutch VOC to Britain.

questions.question: Expanding European settlement usually led to:
questions.memo: Expanding settlement increased conflict with indigenous communities.

questions.question: The early ____ century is when Britain expanded settlement at the Cape.
questions.memo: British expansion at the Cape took off in the early 19th century.

questions.question: British settlers had no impact on the eastern frontier.
questions.memo: British settlers added to land pressure and frontier conflict.

questions.question: The arrival of the British is an example of:
options: A change in who held power
questions.expected: A change in who held power
questions.memo: It marked a change in colonial power at the Cape.

SSSP.G7.H4.A2.title: The eastern frontier
SSSP.G7.H4.A2.description: History (CAPS G7 T4) — Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C): The eastern frontier.
SSSP.G7.H4.A2.caps_topic: Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C)
SSSP.G7.H4.A2.recovery_strategy: The eastern frontier = repeated wars between settlers and the Xhosa.

questions.question: The frontier wars on the eastern frontier were mainly between settlers and which people?
questions.memo: The eastern frontier saw repeated wars between European settlers and the Xhosa.

questions.question: Chief Maqoma (1798–1873) is remembered for what?
options: Leading Xhosa resistance to British rule
questions.expected: Leading Xhosa resistance to British rule
questions.memo: Maqoma was a Xhosa leader who resisted British expansion on the eastern frontier.

questions.question: Andries Stockenström was a colonial official involved on the eastern frontier.
questions.memo: Stockenström was a soldier and official deeply involved in eastern-frontier affairs.

questions.question: The Great Trek was the movement of which group into the interior?
questions.memo: The Great Trek saw Boers (Dutch-descended farmers) move into the interior, away from British rule.

questions.question: Slavery was abolished in the British Cape in which year?
questions.memo: Britain abolished slavery in the Cape in 1836, a major change for the colony.

questions.question: The eastern frontier was peaceful, with no conflict between settlers and the Xhosa.
questions.memo: The eastern frontier was marked by repeated frontier wars between settlers and the Xhosa.

questions.question: Repeated wars between settlers and the Xhosa on the eastern frontier are called ____ wars.
questions.memo: These conflicts over land on the colony's edge are known as the frontier wars.

questions.question: What were most frontier wars fundamentally about?
questions.memo: At their heart, the frontier wars were struggles over land between settlers and the Xhosa.

questions.question: Why did some Boers leave the Cape on the Great Trek?
options: To escape British rule and find new land
questions.expected: To escape British rule and find new land
questions.memo: Many Boers trekked inland to escape British control and seek land of their own.

questions.question: The frontier wars were fought over control of:
questions.memo: The frontier wars were struggles over land and cattle.

questions.question: Chief Maqoma was a Xhosa leader who resisted the British.
questions.memo: Maqoma led Xhosa resistance against British expansion.

questions.question: The Great Trek took the Boers away from the Cape to escape:
questions.memo: Many Boers trekked inland to escape British control.

questions.question: Slavery was abolished in the British Cape in ____.
questions.memo: Britain abolished Cape slavery in 1836.

questions.question: The abolition of slavery angered some Boer slave-owners.
questions.memo: Ending slavery angered Boer slave-owners, a factor behind the Great Trek.

questions.question: Andries Stockenström was a colonial:
questions.memo: Stockenström was a colonial official and soldier on the eastern frontier.

questions.question: The repeated wars on the eastern frontier show a relationship of:
questions.memo: The eastern frontier was defined by repeated conflict over land.

questions.question: The Xhosa simply gave up their land without resistance.
questions.memo: The Xhosa resisted strongly in a series of frontier wars.

questions.question: Inboekselings were people who were:
questions.memo: Inboekselings were people, often children, bound into forced labour.

questions.question: The ____ resisted British rule on the eastern frontier.
questions.memo: The Xhosa led resistance on the eastern frontier.

questions.question: The Great Trek moved Boers into the interior of southern Africa.
questions.memo: The Great Trek took Boers inland, away from the British Cape.

questions.question: A 'case study' like Maqoma helps us:
options: Understand the bigger story through one example
questions.expected: Understand the bigger story through one example
questions.memo: A case study uses one example to illuminate the wider history.

SSSP.G7.H4.A3.title: The northern frontier
SSSP.G7.H4.A3.description: History (CAPS G7 T4) — Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C): The northern frontier.
SSSP.G7.H4.A3.caps_topic: Conflict on the Cape frontiers (early 19th C)
SSSP.G7.H4.A3.recovery_strategy: Northern frontier = trade and mission contact, not just war.

questions.question: Who were the Griqua?
options: People of mixed descent who traded on the northern frontier
questions.expected: People of mixed descent who traded on the northern frontier
questions.memo: The Griqua were communities of mixed descent and runaway slaves who traded on the northern frontier.

questions.question: Trade was an important feature of the northern frontier of European settlement.
questions.memo: The northern frontier was shaped by trade between the Kora, Griqua, Tswana and the Cape.

questions.question: The Tswana traded which goods with the Kora and Griqua?
questions.memo: The Tswana traded ivory, hides, skins, iron and copper on the northern frontier.

questions.question: Robert Moffat (1795–1883) worked at Kuruman as a what?
questions.memo: Robert Moffat was a missionary based at Kuruman on the northern frontier.

questions.question: Some Tswana towns of the early 19th century were among the largest settlements in southern Africa.
questions.memo: Towns like Kaditshwene held thousands of people — among the largest in the region at the time.

questions.question: On the northern frontier, ____ and missionaries were important alongside traders.
questions.memo: Griqua traders and missionaries shaped contact on the northern frontier.

questions.question: How did the northern frontier differ from the eastern frontier?
options: It was shaped more by trade and missions than by repeated wars
questions.expected: It was shaped more by trade and missions than by repeated wars
questions.memo: The northern frontier was marked more by trade and mission contact than the eastern frontier's wars.

questions.question: Manufactured goods, tobacco and pack oxen were traded FROM the Cape to which groups?
questions.memo: The Kora and Griqua traded Cape goods like tobacco and oxen on the northern frontier.

questions.question: Missionaries had no role on the northern frontier.
questions.memo: Missionaries such as Robert Moffat played an important role on the northern frontier.

questions.question: The Kora and Griqua often included:
options: People of mixed descent and runaway slaves
questions.expected: People of mixed descent and runaway slaves
questions.memo: The Kora and Griqua were communities of mixed descent and runaway slaves.

questions.question: The Tswana built large stone-walled towns on the northern frontier.
questions.memo: Tswana towns of stone, like Kaditshwene, were among the region's largest settlements.

questions.question: Robert Moffat was based at which mission station?
questions.memo: Moffat worked at the Kuruman mission station.

questions.question: The Tswana traded ivory, hides, iron and ____ on the northern frontier.
questions.memo: The Tswana traded ivory, hides, iron and copper.

questions.question: The northern frontier was shaped mainly by trade and missions.
questions.memo: Trade and missionary contact, more than war, shaped the northern frontier.

questions.question: Some Tswana towns held thousands of people, showing they were:
questions.memo: Large Tswana towns prove these were big, organised African settlements.

questions.question: Missionaries on the frontier often also acted as:
options: A link for trade and contact
questions.expected: A link for trade and contact
questions.memo: Missionaries were often a point of trade and contact between groups.

questions.question: Only Cape Town was a similar size to the largest Tswana towns at the time.
questions.memo: By 1820 only Cape Town rivalled the biggest Tswana towns in size.

questions.question: Goods like tobacco and pack oxen came from the Cape to the:
questions.memo: The Kora and Griqua traded Cape goods like tobacco and oxen.

questions.question: Robert Moffat worked as a ____ at Kuruman.
questions.memo: Moffat was a missionary at Kuruman.

questions.question: The northern frontier had no large African settlements.
questions.memo: Large Tswana towns showed the northern frontier had big African settlements.

questions.question: Comparing the eastern and northern frontiers shows that contact could mean:
questions.memo: Frontiers involved both conflict and trade, in different mixes.

SSSP.G7.G1.A1.title: Local and street maps
SSSP.G7.G1.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T1) — Map skills (local maps): Local and street maps.
SSSP.G7.G1.A1.recovery_strategy: Grid reference: read along the bottom first, then up the side.

questions.question: On a street map, what do the lines forming a grid help you to do?
options: Find and describe the location of places
questions.expected: Find and describe the location of places
questions.memo: A grid divides the map into blocks so you can give and find the location of places.

questions.question: A map index helps you find which grid block a place is in.
questions.memo: The index lists places with a grid reference so you can look them up quickly on the map.

questions.question: To read a grid reference, you read along the bottom first, then ____.
questions.memo: Grid references go 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — across the bottom, then up the side.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a street map?
options: To show roads and help you find places and routes
To show the layers of the earth
questions.expected: To show roads and help you find places and routes
questions.memo: A street map shows roads and places so you can locate them and plan routes.

questions.question: A street guide's index usually lists places in alphabetical order with a grid reference.
questions.memo: Indexes are alphabetical and give each place a grid reference for quick finding.

questions.question: If a place is listed as 'C4' in the index, what does C4 tell you?
options: The grid block where you will find it
questions.expected: The grid block where you will find it
questions.memo: A reference like C4 points to the grid block on the map where the place is found.

questions.question: Why are local and street maps useful in everyday life?
options: They help people find places and plan journeys
They show the whole world at once
questions.expected: They help people find places and plan journeys
questions.memo: Local maps help with everyday tasks like finding an address or planning a route.

questions.question: You can use a street map to describe a route from one place to another.
questions.memo: Following streets on the map, you can describe the route a person should take.

questions.question: A map symbol is:
options: A small picture standing for a real feature
questions.expected: A small picture standing for a real feature
questions.memo: Symbols are small pictures that stand for real features; the key explains them.

questions.question: A street map usually shows the names of roads.
questions.memo: Street maps label roads so you can find and follow them.

questions.question: To find a place quickly in a street guide you use the:
questions.memo: The index lists places with grid references for quick finding.

questions.question: A grid divides a map into ____ to help locate places.
questions.memo: The grid splits the map into blocks for easy reference.

questions.question: Local maps are useful for finding your way in your own area.
questions.memo: Local maps help you find places and routes in your own area.

questions.question: Reading a grid reference, the first letter or number usually refers to the:
questions.memo: You read across (column) first, then up (row).

questions.question: Which is most useful for finding a friend's house in a suburb?
questions.memo: A local street map shows the detail you need to find a house.

questions.question: A map's key and grid work together to help you find places.
questions.memo: The key explains symbols and the grid locates them — together they help you read the map.

questions.question: A place at grid reference B2 will be found:
options: In block B2 of the grid
questions.expected: In block B2 of the grid
questions.memo: B2 points to the block where column B and row 2 meet.

questions.question: The list of places with their grid references is the map's ____.
questions.memo: The index lists places and their grid references.

questions.question: You can describe a route by naming the streets to follow on a map.
questions.memo: Following the streets on a map, you can describe a route clearly.

questions.question: Street maps are an example of which kind of map?
questions.memo: Street maps are large-scale maps of a small local area.

SSSP.G7.G1.A2.title: Sketch maps and routes
SSSP.G7.G1.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T1) — Map skills (local maps): Sketch maps and routes.
SSSP.G7.G1.A2.recovery_strategy: A good sketch map needs a key, a scale and a north arrow.

questions.question: Which three things should a good sketch map include?
options: A key, a scale and a north arrow
A photo, a date and a price
A graph, a table and a title only
questions.expected: A key, a scale and a north arrow
questions.memo: A clear sketch map needs a key (to explain symbols), a scale and a north arrow.

questions.question: A north arrow on a map shows which direction is north.
questions.memo: The north arrow tells you which way is north so you can work out other directions.

questions.question: If north is at the top of the map, which direction is on the right?
questions.memo: With north at the top: right is east, left is west, bottom is south. ('Never Eat Soggy Worms' = N, E, S, W clockwise.)

questions.question: The four main compass directions are north, south, east and ____.
questions.memo: North, south, east and west are the four cardinal (main) compass directions.

questions.question: A 'key' (legend) on a sketch map does what?
questions.memo: The key (legend) explains what each symbol on the map stands for.

questions.question: When explaining a route, it helps to use compass directions and estimate distances.
questions.memo: Good route directions use compass directions ('go east') and rough distances ('about 2 km').

questions.question: Put these directions for a route in a sensible order from start to finish.

items.text: Arrive at the clinic on your left

questions.memo: Clear route directions go step by step from the start point to the destination.

questions.question: Which direction is exactly opposite to east?
questions.memo: East and west are opposites, as are north and south.

questions.question: If you face north, south is:
questions.memo: Facing north, south is directly behind you.

questions.question: Northeast is the direction between north and east.
questions.memo: Northeast lies halfway between north and east.

questions.question: A sketch map is:
questions.memo: A sketch map is a simple drawing showing the main features.

questions.question: On most maps, ____ is at the top.
questions.memo: By convention, north is at the top of most maps.

questions.question: Estimating distances helps when giving someone directions.
questions.memo: Telling someone roughly how far to go makes directions clearer.

questions.question: Which direction is between south and west?
questions.memo: Southwest lies between south and west.

questions.question: A key on a sketch map should explain the:
questions.memo: The key explains the symbols drawn on the map.

questions.question: A sketch map does not need to be perfectly to scale to be useful.
questions.memo: Sketch maps show the main idea simply; they need not be exactly to scale.

questions.question: To turn from facing east to facing north you turn:
questions.memo: From east, turning left (anti-clockwise) faces you north.

questions.question: The four main directions are north, east, south and ____.
questions.memo: North, east, south and west are the four cardinal directions.

questions.question: A north arrow and a key make a sketch map easier to read.
questions.memo: A north arrow and key help others understand your sketch map.

questions.question: Good route directions include:
questions.memo: Clear directions give turns, compass directions and rough distances.

SSSP.G7.G1.A3.title: Distance and scale
SSSP.G7.G1.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T1) — Map skills (local maps): Distance and scale.
SSSP.G7.G1.A3.recovery_strategy: Use string for a winding road, a ruler for a straight line, then read the scale.

questions.question: What does the scale of a map tell you?
options: How distances on the map relate to real distances
questions.expected: How distances on the map relate to real distances
questions.memo: Scale links a distance on the map to the real distance on the ground.

questions.question: A line scale (bar scale) lets you measure real distances on a map.
questions.memo: You compare a distance on the map to the line scale to read off the real distance.

questions.question: To measure the distance of a winding road on a map, the best tool is:
questions.memo: Lay string along the winding road, then straighten it against the scale to get the distance.

questions.question: A ____ scale uses words, such as '1 cm represents 1 km'.
questions.memo: A word scale states the relationship in words, e.g. '1 cm represents 1 km'.

questions.question: A 'large-scale' map shows a small area with:
questions.memo: Large-scale maps zoom in on a small area and show lots of detail.

questions.question: You should always check a distance you estimated by measuring it accurately.
questions.memo: Estimating first and then measuring accurately is good practice for map distances.

questions.question: If a map's word scale says '1 cm represents 2 km', how far is 3 cm on the map in real life?
questions.memo: 3 cm × 2 km per cm = 6 km on the ground.

questions.question: A straight-line (direct) route between two places is usually shorter than a winding road between them.
questions.memo: The direct line is the shortest distance; a winding road covers more ground.

questions.question: On a map with scale '1 cm = 5 km', 4 cm represents:
questions.memo: 4 cm × 5 km per cm = 20 km.

questions.question: A small-scale map shows a large area with less detail.
questions.memo: Small-scale maps cover large areas but show less detail.

questions.question: A line scale (bar scale) is useful because you can:
questions.memo: You measure a map distance and compare it to the line scale.

questions.question: Scale links map distance to ____ distance.
questions.memo: Scale connects distance on the map to the real distance on the ground.

questions.question: A direct route is a straight line between two points.
questions.memo: A direct route is the straight-line distance between two places.

questions.question: To measure a curved river's length you would use:
questions.memo: String follows the curves, then is measured against the scale.

questions.question: On scale '1 cm = 2 km', a road measuring 5 cm is really:
questions.memo: 5 cm × 2 km per cm = 10 km.

questions.question: Estimating then measuring helps you check your answer.
questions.memo: Estimating first lets you check whether your measured answer is sensible.

questions.question: Which map would show more detail of one school?
questions.memo: Large-scale maps show small areas in greater detail.

questions.question: A ____ scale draws a marked line you measure against.
questions.memo: A line (bar) scale is a marked line for measuring distances.

questions.question: Different maps can use different scales.
questions.memo: Maps use different scales depending on the area and detail needed.

questions.question: Why is scale important on a map?
options: It lets you work out real distances
questions.expected: It lets you work out real distances
questions.memo: Without scale you could not work out real distances from a map.

SSSP.G7.G1.A4.title: Places in the news
SSSP.G7.G1.A4.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T1) — Map skills (local maps): Places in the news.
SSSP.G7.G1.A4.recovery_strategy: Latitude = how far north/south; longitude = how far east/west.

questions.question: Lines of latitude on a globe run in which direction?
questions.memo: Lines of latitude run east–west and measure how far north or south a place is.

questions.question: Lines of longitude measure how far ____ a place is.
questions.memo: Lines of longitude run north–south and measure how far east or west a place is.

questions.question: Latitude and longitude together can give the exact location of a place in the news.
questions.memo: A latitude and a longitude cross at one point, pinpointing a place's exact location.

questions.question: The line of latitude at 0° is called the ____.
questions.memo: The equator is the 0° line of latitude, halfway between the poles.

questions.question: Why is it useful to locate places in the news on a world map?
options: It helps you understand where events happen and why
questions.expected: It helps you understand where events happen and why
questions.memo: Placing news events on a map builds understanding of where and why things happen.

questions.question: Degrees are the units used to measure latitude and longitude.
questions.memo: Latitude and longitude are measured in degrees (°).

questions.question: A place's latitude tells you how far it is from which line?
questions.memo: Latitude measures distance north or south of the equator.

questions.question: Lines of latitude include the equator at:
questions.memo: The equator is the 0° line of latitude.

questions.question: Longitude lines run from the North Pole to the South Pole.
questions.memo: Lines of longitude run north–south, between the poles.

questions.question: A place north of the equator has a latitude that is:
questions.memo: Places north of the equator have northern latitudes.

questions.question: Latitude and longitude are measured in ____.
questions.memo: Both are measured in degrees.

questions.question: Knowing a place's latitude and longitude lets you find it on any world map.
questions.memo: Latitude and longitude together pinpoint a place anywhere on Earth.

questions.question: Following news events on a map helps you understand:
questions.memo: Mapping the news builds understanding of where and why events occur.

questions.question: The line of longitude at 0 degrees is the:
questions.memo: The Prime Meridian is the 0° line of longitude.

questions.question: South Africa lies south of the equator.
questions.memo: South Africa is in the Southern Hemisphere, south of the equator.

questions.question: A grid of latitude and longitude covers:
questions.memo: Latitude and longitude form a grid over the entire globe.

questions.question: The ____ divides the Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
questions.memo: The equator separates the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.question: A latitude of 0° and longitude of 0° is a single point on Earth.
questions.memo: Where the equator and Prime Meridian cross is one exact point.

questions.question: Why are world maps useful for the news?
options: They put global events in their place
questions.expected: They put global events in their place
questions.memo: World maps help locate and make sense of global news events.

SSSP.G7.G2.A1.title: Structure of the earth
SSSP.G7.G2.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T2) — Volcanoes, earthquakes & floods: Structure of the earth.
SSSP.G7.G2.A1.recovery_strategy: Three layers: crust (thin skin), mantle (thick middle), core (hot centre).

questions.question: What are the three main layers of the earth, from outside to inside?
questions.memo: From outside in: crust (thin skin), mantle (thick middle), core (hot centre).

questions.question: The crust is the thin outer layer of the earth.
questions.memo: The crust is the earth's thin, solid outer skin, where we live.

questions.question: The earth's crust is broken into large pieces called tectonic ____.
