questions.memo: The crust is split into tectonic plates that slowly move.

questions.question: The hot centre of the earth is called the:
questions.memo: The core is the very hot centre of the earth.

questions.question: Order the earth's layers from the surface down to the centre.
questions.memo: From the surface inward: crust, then mantle, then core.

questions.question: Tectonic plates move very quickly, several metres every day.
questions.memo: Tectonic plates move extremely slowly — only a few centimetres a year.

questions.question: Why does the movement of tectonic plates matter for this topic?
questions.memo: Plate movements at plate edges cause most volcanoes and earthquakes.

questions.question: The mantle is the layer:
options: Between the crust and the core
questions.expected: Between the crust and the core
questions.memo: The mantle is the thick layer between crust and core.

questions.question: The crust is thin compared with the layers below it.
questions.memo: The crust is a thin skin compared with the much thicker mantle and core.

questions.question: The core is described as:
questions.memo: The core is the very hot centre of the Earth.

questions.question: The Earth's outer layer is the ____.
questions.memo: The crust is the outer layer where we live.

questions.question: Tectonic plates are pieces of the crust.
questions.memo: The crust is broken into moving tectonic plates.

questions.question: Plate movements happen:
questions.memo: Plates move only a few centimetres a year — very slowly.

questions.question: Earthquakes and volcanoes are linked to:
questions.memo: Both are caused by movements at plate boundaries.

questions.question: The crust is the hottest layer of the Earth.
questions.memo: The core, not the crust, is the hottest layer.

questions.question: Which order is correct from outside to centre?
questions.memo: Outside to centre: crust, mantle, core.

questions.question: Pieces of the crust that move are called tectonic ____.
questions.memo: The moving crustal pieces are tectonic plates.

questions.question: Understanding the Earth's layers helps explain volcanoes and earthquakes.
questions.memo: Knowing about plates and layers explains why volcanoes and earthquakes occur.

questions.question: Most volcanic and earthquake activity occurs:
questions.memo: Activity concentrates at the edges where plates meet.

SSSP.G7.G2.A2.title: Volcanoes
SSSP.G7.G2.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T2) — Volcanoes, earthquakes & floods: Volcanoes.
SSSP.G7.G2.A2.recovery_strategy: Volcanoes line up along the edges of tectonic plates.

questions.question: Where do most volcanoes occur?
options: Along the edges of tectonic plates
In the middle of flat plains
questions.expected: Along the edges of tectonic plates
questions.memo: Most volcanoes line up along tectonic plate boundaries.

questions.question: A volcano is an opening in the earth's crust where molten rock can reach the surface.
questions.memo: Volcanoes are openings where magma (molten rock) erupts onto the surface.

questions.question: Molten rock below the surface is called magma; once it erupts it is called ____.
questions.memo: Underground it is magma; once it pours out it is called lava.

questions.question: Volcanoes occur because of activity linked to what?
questions.memo: Volcanic activity is driven by plate movements deep in the earth.

questions.question: Volcanoes and earthquakes often happen in the same regions.
questions.memo: Both cluster along plate boundaries, so they often occur in the same areas.

questions.question: On a world map, the pattern of volcanoes mostly matches the pattern of what?
questions.memo: Mapping volcanoes reveals the lines of the plate boundaries.

questions.question: Which is a possible effect of a volcanic eruption?
options: Lava and ash damaging the area
questions.expected: Lava and ash damaging the area
questions.memo: Eruptions can bury land in lava and ash, causing serious local damage.

questions.question: When a volcano erupts, lava is:
questions.memo: Lava is molten rock that flows out during an eruption.

questions.question: Volcanic ash can be thrown high into the air during an eruption.
questions.memo: Eruptions can blast ash high into the atmosphere.

questions.question: Volcanoes mostly form:
options: In the middle of flat plains
questions.memo: Volcanoes mostly form where tectonic plates meet.

questions.question: Molten rock underground is called ____.
questions.memo: Underground it is magma; once erupted it becomes lava.

questions.question: Volcanic eruptions can destroy homes and farmland nearby.
questions.memo: Lava and ash can bury and destroy nearby homes and farmland.

questions.question: A map of the world's volcanoes shows them:
questions.memo: Volcanoes line up along the plate boundaries.

questions.question: Why do volcanoes form where plates meet?
options: Magma can rise through gaps and weaknesses
questions.expected: Magma can rise through gaps and weaknesses
questions.memo: At plate edges, magma can rise through cracks and erupt.

questions.question: Volcanic soil can be very fertile for farming.
questions.memo: Weathered volcanic ash makes rich, fertile soil for farming.

questions.question: An advantage that draws people to live near volcanoes is:
questions.memo: Fertile volcanic soil attracts farmers despite the risk.

questions.question: A volcano is an opening where molten rock reaches the ____.
questions.memo: A volcano is where magma reaches the Earth's surface.

questions.question: Volcanoes never occur near earthquakes.
questions.memo: Volcanoes and earthquakes often occur together along plate boundaries.

questions.question: Studying volcano locations helps people to:
options: Understand and prepare for the hazard
questions.expected: Understand and prepare for the hazard
questions.memo: Knowing where volcanoes are helps communities prepare.

SSSP.G7.G2.A3.title: Earthquakes
SSSP.G7.G2.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T2) — Volcanoes, earthquakes & floods: Earthquakes.
SSSP.G7.G2.A3.recovery_strategy: Earthquakes happen where plates grind past each other.

questions.question: What causes earthquakes?
questions.memo: Earthquakes happen when tectonic plates move or grind against each other.

questions.question: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground.
questions.memo: An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement in the crust.

questions.question: Which of these can be an effect of a strong earthquake?
options: Damaged buildings and loss of life
questions.expected: Damaged buildings and loss of life
questions.memo: Earthquakes can destroy buildings and infrastructure and cause injury and loss of life.

questions.question: An undersea earthquake can cause a giant wave called a ____.
questions.memo: A tsunami is a huge wave that can be triggered by an undersea earthquake.

questions.question: Why are some communities at higher risk from earthquakes than others?
options: They are near plate boundaries or have weaker buildings
They are far from the sea
questions.expected: They are near plate boundaries or have weaker buildings
questions.memo: Risk is higher near plate boundaries and where buildings are not built to resist shaking.

questions.question: There is nothing people can do to reduce the impact of earthquakes.
questions.memo: People reduce impact by building stronger structures, planning and preparing emergency responses.

questions.question: Sort each item as a CAUSE or an EFFECT of an earthquake.

items.text: Tectonic plates grinding past each other
Movement deep in the earth's crust

questions.expected: Plate movement is the cause; collapsed buildings and displaced people are effects.
questions.memo: Causes come from plate movement; effects are the damage and disruption that follow.

questions.question: Preparing for earthquakes (drills, strong buildings) is an example of what?
options: Reducing the impact of a hazard
questions.expected: Reducing the impact of a hazard
questions.memo: Preparation and strong building reduce the impact when an earthquake strikes.

questions.question: Earthquakes happen when plates:
questions.memo: A sudden slip of plates releases energy as an earthquake.

questions.question: Strong earthquakes can damage roads, bridges and buildings.
questions.memo: Earthquakes can destroy infrastructure like roads, bridges and buildings.

questions.question: After an earthquake, people may be displaced, meaning they:
options: Lose their homes and must move
questions.expected: Lose their homes and must move
questions.memo: Displacement means losing homes and having to move away.

questions.question: An undersea earthquake may trigger a giant wave called a ____.
questions.memo: Undersea quakes can cause tsunamis.

questions.question: Stronger buildings can reduce earthquake damage.
questions.memo: Buildings designed to resist shaking reduce damage and save lives.

questions.question: Communities near plate boundaries are at higher earthquake risk because:
options: That is where most earthquakes happen
They are far from the sea
questions.expected: That is where most earthquakes happen
questions.memo: Most earthquakes occur at plate boundaries, raising local risk.

questions.question: An earthquake drill helps people to:
options: Know what to do and stay safer
questions.expected: Know what to do and stay safer
questions.memo: Practising drills helps people respond safely when a quake strikes.

questions.question: Nothing can be done to prepare for earthquakes.
questions.memo: Strong buildings, drills and planning all help communities prepare.

questions.question: Earthquakes can cause fires when they:
options: Break gas pipes and power lines
questions.expected: Break gas pipes and power lines
questions.memo: Broken gas and power lines can spark fires after a quake.

questions.question: Earthquakes are caused by movement in the Earth's ____.
questions.memo: Movement in the crust at plate boundaries causes earthquakes.

questions.question: Disease can spread after an earthquake if water and sanitation are damaged.
questions.memo: Damaged water and sanitation after a quake can spread disease.

questions.question: Why do some earthquakes cause more deaths than others of similar size?
questions.memo: Weaker buildings and poor preparation lead to more deaths.

SSSP.G7.G2.A4.title: Floods
SSSP.G7.G2.A4.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T2) — Volcanoes, earthquakes & floods: Floods.
SSSP.G7.G2.A4.recovery_strategy: Floods worsen when land can't soak up or carry away the water.

questions.question: Which of these is a common cause of floods?
questions.memo: Heavy rain is a leading cause of floods, especially when the land cannot absorb it.

questions.question: Removing vegetation can make flooding worse.
questions.memo: Without plants to soak up and slow water, rain runs off faster and flooding worsens.

questions.question: Which is an effect of a serious flood?
options: Damage to homes and loss of life
questions.expected: Damage to homes and loss of life
questions.memo: Floods can damage homes, fields and infrastructure and cause injury, disease and loss of life.

questions.question: When soil is washed away by flood water, this is called soil ____.
questions.memo: Flood water washing soil away is soil erosion, which harms farmland.

questions.question: Building on a floodplain can put people at higher risk of flooding.
questions.memo: Settling on low land near rivers (floodplains) increases the risk of being flooded.

questions.question: How can a community reduce the impact of floods?
options: Early warnings, drainage and avoiding building on floodplains
questions.expected: Early warnings, drainage and avoiding building on floodplains
questions.memo: Warnings, good drainage and sensible building reduce flood impact.

questions.question: Besides heavy rain, which event can also cause flooding?
options: A tsunami from an undersea earthquake
A cold front with no rain
questions.expected: A tsunami from an undersea earthquake
questions.memo: Tsunamis (from undersea earthquakes) can flood coastal areas.

questions.question: Floods can spread disease as well as damage property.
questions.memo: Dirty flood water can spread disease, on top of damaging homes and fields.

questions.question: A flood happens when:
options: Water covers land that is usually dry
questions.expected: Water covers land that is usually dry
questions.memo: A flood is water covering normally dry land.

questions.question: Cutting down forests can increase the risk of flooding.
questions.memo: Without trees to soak up and slow water, flooding becomes more likely.

questions.question: A floodplain is:
options: Low, flat land near a river that floods
questions.expected: Low, flat land near a river that floods
questions.memo: Floodplains are low areas beside rivers that flood easily.

questions.question: Early warning systems help reduce the ____ of floods.
questions.memo: Warnings help people prepare, reducing flood impact.

questions.question: Floods can damage crops and cause food shortages.
questions.memo: Floods can ruin crops, leading to food shortages.

questions.question: Why do some communities suffer more from floods?
options: They live on floodplains or have weak defences
questions.expected: They live on floodplains or have weak defences
questions.memo: Living on floodplains with weak defences raises flood risk.

questions.question: Good drainage helps prevent floods by:
questions.memo: Drainage channels carry water away, reducing flooding.

questions.question: Dirty flood water can make people sick.
questions.memo: Flood water often carries dirt and disease that can make people sick.

questions.question: A South African flood case study should be:
options: A real flood that happened in South Africa
questions.expected: A real flood that happened in South Africa
questions.memo: CAPS asks for a real South African flood case study.

questions.question: Planting trees and keeping vegetation can ____ flood risk.
questions.memo: Vegetation soaks up and slows water, lowering flood risk.

questions.question: People can do nothing to reduce flood damage.
questions.memo: Warnings, drainage, vegetation and wise building all reduce flood damage.

questions.question: Floods and droughts are both examples of:
questions.memo: Both floods and droughts are water-related natural hazards.

SSSP.G7.G3.A1.title: Population concepts
SSSP.G7.G3.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T3) — Population growth & change: Population concepts.
SSSP.G7.G3.A1.recovery_strategy: Growth rate = births minus deaths (ignoring migration).

questions.question: The birth rate measures the number of:
options: Babies born per 1 000 people per year
questions.expected: Babies born per 1 000 people per year
questions.memo: Birth rate = the number of live births per 1 000 people in a year.

questions.question: The death rate measures the number of:
questions.memo: Death rate = the number of deaths per 1 000 people in a year.

questions.question: Population growth happens when the birth rate is higher than the death rate.
questions.memo: If more are born than die, the population grows (ignoring migration).

questions.question: ____ mortality rate is the number of babies who die before their first birthday.
questions.memo: Infant mortality measures deaths of babies under one year old.

questions.question: Life expectancy is:
options: The average number of years a person is expected to live
questions.expected: The average number of years a person is expected to live
questions.memo: Life expectancy is the average lifespan people in a place can expect.

questions.question: A high infant mortality rate usually points to poorer health conditions.
questions.memo: Many babies dying young usually signals poorer health care and living conditions.

questions.question: A country has a birth rate of 30 and a death rate of 10 per 1 000. Is its population growing or shrinking?
questions.memo: Births (30) are higher than deaths (10), so the population is growing.

questions.question: Which two measures are subtracted to find natural population growth?
questions.memo: Natural growth = birth rate − death rate (migration is separate).

questions.question: If births are fewer than deaths, the population will:
questions.memo: Fewer births than deaths means the population shrinks.

questions.question: Life expectancy tends to be higher where health care is good.
questions.memo: Good health care raises life expectancy.

questions.question: Infant mortality measures the death of:
questions.memo: Infant mortality counts deaths of babies under one year.

questions.question: Birth rate and death rate are measured per ____ people.
questions.memo: Both are measured per 1 000 people per year.

questions.question: Population can also change because of people moving in or out (migration).
questions.memo: Migration changes population, alongside births and deaths.

questions.question: A country with birth rate 12 and death rate 12 has natural growth of:
questions.memo: 12 births minus 12 deaths = zero natural growth.

questions.question: Life expectancy of 80 means people can expect to live to about:
questions.memo: Life expectancy of 80 means an average lifespan of about 80 years.

questions.question: Higher death rates always mean a falling population.
questions.memo: A high birth rate can outweigh a high death rate, so population may still grow.

questions.question: Population growth rate tells us:
options: How fast a population is changing
questions.expected: How fast a population is changing
questions.memo: Growth rate shows how fast a population is rising or falling.

questions.question: The average number of years people live is called life ____.
questions.memo: Life expectancy is the average lifespan.

questions.question: These measures help us compare different countries' populations.

questions.question: A very high infant mortality rate is a sign of:
questions.memo: High infant mortality usually signals poor health conditions.

SSSP.G7.G3.A2.recovery_strategy: Ask of each factor: does it push births/deaths up or down?

questions.question: Which of these can lower the death rate in a country?
questions.memo: Improved health care helps people live longer, lowering the death rate.

questions.question: Widespread disease such as HIV/AIDS or malaria can raise the death rate.
questions.memo: Serious widespread illness raises the death rate.

questions.memo: Government policy can encourage or limit births, changing the birth rate.

questions.question: Wars and conflict tend to ____ the death rate.

questions.question: Family needs, attitudes and beliefs mainly influence which rate?

questions.question: Better economic status and wealth often lead families to have fewer children.
questions.memo: In wealthier conditions, families often choose to have fewer children, lowering the birth rate.

questions.question: Why might a high risk of death lead to a higher birth rate in some societies?
options: Families may have more children expecting some may not survive
questions.expected: Families may have more children expecting some may not survive

questions.question: Clean water and sanitation tend to:

questions.question: The Black Death was a pandemic that raised death rates in the past.

questions.question: In wealthier societies, families often have:

questions.question: HIV/AIDS, malaria and ____ are diseases that affect death rates.

questions.question: Government policy can encourage or discourage having children.

questions.question: War usually affects population by:

questions.question: Improved medicine usually:
questions.memo: Better medicine keeps people alive longer, lowering death rates.

questions.question: Beliefs and attitudes can influence how many children families want.

questions.question: Why are birth and death rates sometimes linked?
options: High child death can lead families to have more children
questions.expected: High child death can lead families to have more children
questions.memo: Where child death is common, families may have more children — the rates interact.

questions.question: A widespread disease outbreak is called a ____.
questions.memo: A pandemic is a widespread disease outbreak that raises death rates.

questions.question: Economic conditions can influence both birth and death rates.
questions.memo: Wealth and poverty affect both how many children families have and how long people live.

questions.question: Family planning programmes mainly affect the:
questions.memo: Family planning influences how many children are born — the birth rate.

SSSP.G7.G3.A3.title: World population growth
SSSP.G7.G3.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T3) — Population growth & change: World population growth.
SSSP.G7.G3.A3.recovery_strategy: Population stayed flat for ages, then shot up with food, medicine and sanitation.

questions.question: For most of history, world population grew very slowly. When did it start to rise sharply?
options: In the last few hundred years
It has always been the same
questions.expected: In the last few hundred years
questions.memo: World population stayed low for ages, then climbed steeply only in recent centuries.

questions.question: Increased food production helped the world's population to grow.
questions.memo: More food meant fewer people starved, helping the population grow.

questions.question: Which scientific development helped reduce deaths and grow the population?
options: Better control of disease and improved sanitation
questions.expected: Better control of disease and improved sanitation
questions.memo: Understanding disease, better medicine and clean sanitation cut death rates.

questions.question: A line ____ is often used to show how world population has changed over time.
questions.memo: A line graph shows the trend of population over time clearly.

questions.question: Use the data. World population (billions): 1800 → 1, 1927 → 2, 1974 → 4, 2011 → 7. What is the trend?
options: It is rising, and rising faster over time
questions.expected: It is rising, and rising faster over time
questions.memo: The numbers climb and the jumps get bigger and quicker — population is rising at a faster rate.

questions.question: Improved health care was one reason world population grew quickly.
questions.memo: Better health care kept more people alive longer, boosting population growth.

questions.question: Refrigeration and canned food helped population growth by:
questions.memo: Preserving food (canning, refrigeration) reduced spoilage and improved nutrition.

questions.question: Reading a population line graph, a steep upward slope means population is:
questions.memo: A steep upward line on the graph shows rapid population growth.

questions.question: For thousands of years, world population grew:
questions.memo: Population grew slowly for most of history before recent rapid growth.

questions.question: Better farming meant more food and supported more people.
questions.memo: Increased food production allowed the population to grow.

questions.question: Vaccines and medicine helped population grow by:
questions.memo: Controlling disease reduced deaths, helping population grow.

questions.question: A line graph shows population ____ over time.
questions.memo: A line graph shows how population changes over time.

questions.question: World population is now in the billions.
questions.memo: World population has grown into the billions in recent times.

questions.question: On a population graph, a steeper line means:
questions.memo: A steeper upward line means population is growing faster.

questions.question: Refrigeration helped population growth by:
questions.memo: Refrigeration kept food fresh longer, improving nutrition.

questions.question: Improved sanitation helped reduce the spread of disease.
questions.memo: Clean sanitation reduced disease, lowering deaths and aiding growth.

questions.question: The sharp rise in population is mostly due to:
questions.memo: Rapid growth came mainly from falling death rates as health improved.

questions.question: Increased food ____ supported a growing population.
questions.memo: More food production supported more people.

questions.question: Reading graphs is an important geography skill.
questions.memo: Interpreting graphs is a key skill for studying population and other data.

questions.question: Scientific progress affected population mainly by:
questions.memo: Science (medicine, sanitation) helped people live longer, growing the population.

SSSP.G7.G4.A1.title: Natural resources
SSSP.G7.G4.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T4) — Natural resources & conservation (SA): Natural resources.
SSSP.G7.G4.A1.recovery_strategy: A natural resource is something useful we take from nature.

questions.question: Which of these is a natural resource?
questions.memo: Natural resources come from nature — water, air, soil, forests, animals and marine life.

questions.question: Forests, soil and marine life are all natural resources.
questions.memo: Forests, soil, water, air, animals and marine life are all natural resources.

questions.question: 'Abuse' of a natural resource means:
options: Using it in a harmful, wasteful way
questions.expected: Using it in a harmful, wasteful way
questions.memo: Abusing a resource means using it wastefully or in ways that damage it.

questions.question: Air, water, soil and forests are examples of ____ resources.
questions.memo: These all come from nature, so they are natural resources.

questions.question: Why should natural resources be used carefully?
options: So they are not damaged or used up
questions.expected: So they are not damaged or used up
questions.memo: Careful use protects resources so they last and stay healthy.

questions.question: Marine life is an example of a natural resource that can be over-used.
questions.memo: Fish and other marine life can be over-harvested, so they must be used responsibly.

questions.question: Cutting down a whole forest without replanting is an example of:
questions.memo: Destroying a forest without replacing it abuses the resource.

questions.question: Which is NOT a natural resource?
questions.memo: A plastic toy is made by people; water, soil and forests come from nature.

questions.question: Fresh water is a vital natural resource.
questions.memo: Fresh water is one of the most important natural resources.

questions.question: Soil is a natural resource because it:
questions.memo: Soil is a natural resource essential for growing food.

questions.question: Using a resource wastefully and harmfully is called ____ it.
questions.memo: Abusing a resource means using it harmfully or wastefully.

questions.question: Over-fishing can reduce fish populations badly.
questions.memo: Catching fish faster than they breed reduces their populations.

questions.question: Forests provide resources such as:
questions.memo: Forests give wood and shelter for wildlife — natural resources.

questions.question: Wise use of natural resources means:
questions.memo: Wise use protects resources from damage and waste.

questions.question: Air is a natural resource that can be polluted.
questions.memo: Air is a natural resource and can be harmed by pollution.

questions.question: Marine life is found in the:
questions.memo: Marine life lives in the sea and is a natural resource.

questions.question: Water, air, soil and forests are all examples of ____ resources.
questions.memo: These all come from nature, making them natural resources.

questions.question: Natural resources will last forever no matter how we use them.
questions.memo: Many resources can be damaged or used up if not used wisely.

questions.question: Why is it important to look after natural resources?
options: So they stay healthy and available
questions.expected: So they stay healthy and available
questions.memo: Looking after resources keeps them available for everyone, now and later.

SSSP.G7.G4.A2.title: Management and conservation
SSSP.G7.G4.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T4) — Natural resources & conservation (SA): Management and conservation.
SSSP.G7.G4.A2.recovery_strategy: Conservation = using and protecting resources so they last.

questions.question: Conservation means:
options: Protecting and carefully managing the environment and resources
questions.expected: Protecting and carefully managing the environment and resources
questions.memo: Conservation is the careful protection and management of nature and resources.

questions.question: A nature reserve or marine reserve is an example of a conservation area.
questions.memo: Conservation areas, including marine reserves, protect plants, animals and habitats.

questions.question: Eco-tourism is tourism that:
questions.memo: Eco-tourism lets people enjoy nature in ways that support conservation and communities.

questions.question: Setting aside land to protect plants and animals creates a ____ area.
questions.memo: Protected land for nature is a conservation area.

questions.question: A community conservation project usually aims to:
options: Protect nature while benefiting local people
questions.expected: Protect nature while benefiting local people
questions.memo: Community projects protect nature while bringing benefits, such as jobs, to local people.

questions.question: One reason for conservation is to protect resources for future generations.
questions.memo: Conservation keeps resources healthy now and for people in the future.

questions.question: Why might a marine reserve ban fishing in certain areas?
options: To let fish populations recover and survive
questions.expected: To let fish populations recover and survive
questions.memo: No-fishing zones let fish breed and recover, protecting the resource.

questions.question: A national park is an example of a:
questions.memo: National parks protect nature and are conservation areas.

questions.question: Eco-tourism can provide income while protecting nature.
questions.memo: Eco-tourism brings income in ways that support conservation.

questions.question: A marine reserve protects:
questions.memo: Marine reserves protect ocean life and habitats.

questions.question: Protecting and carefully managing nature is called ____.
questions.memo: Conservation is the careful protection and management of nature.

questions.question: Conservation areas can help endangered animals survive.
questions.memo: Protected areas give endangered animals a safer place to survive.

questions.question: Community conservation projects can benefit local people by:
questions.memo: Community projects can create jobs while protecting nature.

questions.question: One reason for conservation is to:
questions.memo: Conservation keeps resources healthy for future generations.

questions.question: Tourists visiting nature reserves can support conservation through fees.
questions.memo: Entry fees from eco-tourism can fund conservation work.

questions.question: Why might fishing be limited in a marine reserve?
questions.memo: Limiting fishing lets fish breed and recover.

questions.question: Tourism that respects and protects nature is called ____-tourism.
questions.memo: Eco-tourism is nature-respecting tourism.

questions.question: Conservation and using resources can be balanced through careful management.
questions.memo: Careful management lets people use resources while conserving them.

questions.question: Conservation areas need a clear:
questions.memo: Conservation areas work best with a clear purpose and management plan.

SSSP.G7.G4.A3.title: Water in South Africa
SSSP.G7.G4.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G7 T4) — Natural resources & conservation (SA): Water in South Africa.
SSSP.G7.G4.A3.recovery_strategy: South Africa is a dry country — water is a scarce, shared resource.

questions.question: South Africa is generally a country with:
options: Limited water — it is fairly dry
questions.expected: Limited water — it is fairly dry
questions.memo: South Africa is a dry country, so water is scarce and must be shared and saved.

questions.question: Looking after catchment areas helps keep rivers healthy.
questions.memo: Catchment areas collect water for rivers, so caring for them protects river health.

questions.question: Which group is a major user of South Africa's water?
questions.memo: Farming is one of the biggest users of South Africa's water, along with industry and homes.

questions.question: Wetlands are disappearing, which is why their ____ is necessary.
questions.memo: Wetlands are valuable and shrinking, so conservation is needed to protect them.

questions.question: Use the pie data. SA water use: agriculture 60%, domestic 25%, industry 15%. Who uses the MOST water?
questions.memo: Agriculture's 60% is the largest share — farming uses the most water.

questions.question: Using water responsibly at home is one way to help conserve South Africa's water.
questions.memo: Domestic users saving water helps conserve the country's scarce supply.

questions.question: Why is wetland conservation important?
options: Wetlands clean water and support wildlife
questions.expected: Wetlands clean water and support wildlife
questions.memo: Wetlands filter and store water and support wildlife, so they are worth protecting.

questions.question: South Africa's water supply is best described as:
questions.memo: South Africa is dry, so water is scarce and must be used carefully.

questions.question: A catchment area collects rainwater that feeds rivers.
questions.memo: Catchment areas gather rainfall that flows into rivers.

questions.question: Wetlands are valuable because they:
options: Store and clean water and support wildlife
questions.expected: Store and clean water and support wildlife
questions.memo: Wetlands store and filter water and shelter wildlife.

questions.question: Farming, industry and ____ users all use South Africa's water.
questions.memo: Agricultural, industrial and domestic (home) users all share the water.

questions.question: Saving water at home helps the whole country's supply.
questions.memo: Every household saving water helps the scarce national supply.

questions.question: Healthy rivers depend on caring for their:
questions.memo: Caring for catchment areas keeps rivers healthy.

questions.question: Why are wetlands disappearing a problem?
options: We lose their water storage and cleaning
questions.expected: We lose their water storage and cleaning
questions.memo: Losing wetlands means losing their water storage and natural cleaning.

questions.question: Agriculture is usually the biggest user of South Africa's water.
questions.memo: Farming is generally the largest user of the country's water.

questions.question: Responsible water use means:
questions.memo: Responsible use means avoiding waste and pollution.

questions.question: In a dry country, water must be ____ and shared carefully.
questions.memo: In a dry country water must be conserved and shared wisely.

questions.question: Industry uses no water in South Africa.
questions.memo: Industry is one of the three main users of water, with farming and homes.

questions.question: Conserving wetlands and catchments helps ensure:
options: A reliable water supply for the future
questions.expected: A reliable water supply for the future
questions.memo: Protecting wetlands and catchments secures future water supply.

SSSP.G8.H1.A1.title: Changes during the Industrial Revolution in Britain
SSSP.G8.H1.A1.description: History (CAPS G8 T1) — The Industrial Revolution (Britain & southern Africa): Changes during the Industrial Revolution in Britain.
SSSP.G8.H1.A1.recovery_strategy: Industrial Revolution = work moves from home/farm to factories and cities.

questions.question: The Industrial Revolution was a change from making goods by hand to making them:
questions.memo: The Industrial Revolution moved production from hand and home into factories using machines.

questions.question: Before the Industrial Revolution, most people worked on farms or in small home industries.
questions.memo: The earlier economy was based on farming and cottage (home) industries.

questions.question: As factories grew, many people moved to cities — a process called ____.
questions.memo: Urbanisation is the growth of cities as people move in for factory work.

questions.question: What were living conditions like for many working-class people during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.memo: Workers often lived in overcrowded, poor housing in the fast-growing industrial cities.

questions.question: Children worked long hours in mills and mines during the Industrial Revolution.
questions.memo: Child labour was common and dangerous in the factories and mines of this period.

questions.question: Workers formed trade unions mainly to:
options: Improve their wages and working conditions
questions.expected: Improve their wages and working conditions
questions.memo: Trade unions organised workers to push for better pay and conditions.

questions.question: The Luddites were workers who protested by:
questions.memo: The Luddites smashed machines they blamed for taking their jobs.

questions.question: The Industrial Revolution increased the wealth and power of Britain.
questions.memo: Industrialisation made Britain richer and more powerful, including as a colonial power.

questions.question: A 'cottage industry' means goods were made:
questions.memo: Cottage industry = small-scale making of goods at home by hand, before factories.

questions.question: The Industrial Revolution began in which country?
questions.memo: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain before spreading.

questions.question: Steam power was an important new technology of the Industrial Revolution.
questions.memo: Steam engines powered factories, mines and transport during the Industrial Revolution.

questions.question: Factories brought many workers together in one place to use:
questions.memo: Factories gathered workers to operate machines under one roof.

questions.question: Many people moved from the countryside to ____ to find factory work.
questions.memo: Workers moved to growing industrial cities for factory jobs.

questions.question: Working-class housing in industrial cities was often overcrowded.
questions.memo: Rapid city growth led to overcrowded, poor working-class housing.

questions.question: Child labour in mills and mines was:
questions.memo: Children worked long, dangerous hours in mills and mines.

questions.question: The Swing Riots were protests by:
questions.memo: The Swing Riots were protests by farm (agricultural) workers.

questions.question: Trade unions were formed to protect workers' interests.
questions.memo: Workers formed unions to push for better wages and conditions.

questions.question: The Grand National Consolidated Trades Union (1833) was an early:
questions.memo: It was an early large-scale workers' union.

questions.question: Before factories, goods were made by hand in small ____ industries.
questions.memo: Cottage industries made goods by hand at home before factories.

questions.question: The Industrial Revolution had both positive and negative effects on people's lives.
questions.memo: It brought new goods and wealth but also poverty, pollution and harsh working conditions.

questions.question: Industrialisation increased Britain's:
questions.memo: Industrialisation made Britain wealthier and more powerful.

SSSP.G8.H1.A2.title: Southern Africa by 1860
SSSP.G8.H1.A2.description: History (CAPS G8 T1) — The Industrial Revolution (Britain & southern Africa): Southern Africa by 1860.
SSSP.G8.H1.A2.recovery_strategy: Indenture = a fixed-term work contract, not slavery but very harsh.

questions.question: Indentured labourers were brought from India to work on sugar plantations in which British colony?
questions.memo: Indian indentured labourers were brought to Natal to work the sugar plantations.

questions.question: Indenture was a fixed-term work contract, often under very harsh conditions.
questions.memo: Indenture bound workers to years of labour under harsh conditions — not slavery, but very hard.

questions.question: Why was labour imported to Natal's sugar plantations?

There were no people in Natal
questions.expected: The independent Zulu kingdom meant local labour was hard to force
questions.memo: With the Zulu kingdom still independent, planters imported indentured Indian labour for the cane fields.

questions.question: Workers bound by a fixed-term contract to labour for years were called ____ labourers.
questions.memo: Indentured labourers worked under binding contracts for a set number of years.

questions.question: 'Passenger Indians' (from 1869) were Indians who came to South Africa:
options: Paying their own way, often as traders

questions.memo: Passenger Indians paid their own passage and often came as traders, unlike indentured labourers.

questions.question: There was a strong demand for sugar in Britain at this time.

questions.question: India at this time was itself ruled as a colony of which country?
questions.memo: India was a British colony, which is why labour could be moved within the empire.

questions.question: Indentured labourers lived and worked in comfortable, easy conditions.
questions.memo: Indentured labourers faced harsh living and working conditions on the plantations.

questions.question: Natal was a British colony.
questions.memo: Natal was under British colonial control.

questions.question: Indentured labourers signed contracts to work for:
questions.memo: Indenture bound workers for a fixed term of years.

questions.question: Indian labour was imported partly because the ____ kingdom was still independent.
questions.memo: With the Zulu kingdom independent, local labour was hard to force, so labour was imported.

questions.question: Some Indians came to South Africa as free 'passenger' immigrants.
questions.memo: Passenger Indians paid their own way, often as traders, unlike indentured labourers.

questions.question: Demand for sugar came mainly from:
questions.memo: British demand for sugar drove Natal's sugar industry.

questions.question: Indentured labourers' conditions were:
questions.memo: Indentured workers faced hard, tightly controlled conditions.

questions.question: Indian immigration added to the diversity of South Africa's population.
questions.memo: Indian immigration contributed to South Africa's diverse population.

questions.question: India and Natal were linked because both were part of the:
questions.memo: Both being in the British Empire allowed labour to move between them.

questions.question: Workers bound by contract for a set term were called ____ labourers.
questions.memo: These were indentured labourers.

questions.question: Passenger Indians were exactly the same as indentured labourers.
questions.memo: Passenger Indians paid their own way and were not bound by indenture contracts.

questions.question: The 'Passenger Indians' arrived from:

SSSP.G8.H1.A3.title: Diamond mining in Kimberley
SSSP.G8.H1.A3.description: History (CAPS G8 T1) — The Industrial Revolution (Britain & southern Africa): Diamond mining in Kimberley.

questions.question: Diamonds were discovered in which South African town in 1867?

questions.question: Diamonds are valuable partly because they are rare and hard.
questions.memo: Diamonds are rare and the hardest natural material, which makes them valuable.

questions.question: As diamond diggings got deeper, what happened to small individual claimholders?
options: Many were squeezed out as big companies took over

questions.memo: Deep mining needed money and machines, so big companies bought out small claimholders.

questions.question: Which company, formed by Cecil John Rhodes, came to dominate diamond mining?
questions.memo: Rhodes's De Beers Consolidated Mines gained a near-monopoly over diamond mining.

questions.memo: A monopoly is control of a market by a single company — as De Beers had with diamonds.

questions.question: Cecil John Rhodes and Barney Barnato were important figures in diamond mining.
questions.memo: Rhodes and Barnato were leading rivals and then partners in the diamond industry.

questions.question: Controlling the supply of diamonds allowed companies to control the:

questions.question: Black claimholders at Kimberley generally:
options: Lost their claims and rights over time
questions.expected: Lost their claims and rights over time
questions.memo: Black claimholders were squeezed out and lost rights as control tightened.

questions.question: Diamond wealth increased Britain's interest in controlling South Africa.
questions.memo: New diamond wealth pulled Britain deeper into controlling the region.

questions.question: Diamonds are valued because they are:
questions.memo: Diamonds are rare and the hardest natural material, making them valuable.

questions.question: As diggings got deeper, mining needed more money and machinery.
questions.memo: Deeper mining required heavy investment, favouring big companies.

questions.question: The 'one person, one claim' rule changed as:
questions.memo: Over time, big companies bought out small claimholders.

questions.question: Cecil John Rhodes formed the company ____ Consolidated Mines.
questions.memo: Rhodes formed De Beers Consolidated Mines.

questions.question: A monopoly let companies control the price of diamonds.
questions.memo: Controlling supply through monopoly let companies keep diamond prices high.

questions.question: Kimberley is famous for its huge man-made hole called the:

questions.question: Diamond wealth increased Britain's interest in:
questions.memo: Diamond wealth pulled Britain toward controlling South Africa.

questions.question: Black claimholders gradually lost their claims and rights.
questions.memo: Black claimholders were squeezed out and lost rights over time.

questions.question: Barney Barnato was, like Rhodes, a:

questions.question: Control of supply by one company is called a ____.
questions.memo: A monopoly is one company's control of supply.

questions.question: Diamond mining began South Africa's Mineral Revolution.
questions.memo: The 1867 diamond find at Kimberley started the Mineral Revolution.

questions.question: Companies regulated the supply of diamonds in order to:
questions.memo: Limiting supply kept diamond prices high and profits large.

SSSP.G8.H2.A1.title: Labour control and land expansion
SSSP.G8.H2.A1.description: History (CAPS G8 T2) — The Mineral Revolution in South Africa: Labour control and land expansion.
SSSP.G8.H2.A1.caps_topic: The Mineral Revolution in South Africa

questions.question: The closed compound system was used to:

questions.memo: By 1879 the Zulu and Pedi were defeated, opening the way for greater labour control.

questions.question: Defeating independent African kingdoms made it easier to force people into mine labour.
questions.memo: Once kingdoms lost independence, men were more easily pushed into migrant mine labour.

questions.question: Land dispossession affected African societies by:

questions.memo: Losing land pushed many African men into wage labour on the mines.

questions.question: The Xhosa were defeated in 1878 as part of:
questions.memo: The 1878 defeat of the Xhosa was part of growing colonial and labour control.

questions.question: Increasing control over black workers was a key feature of the Mineral Revolution.
questions.memo: Tighter control over black labour — compounds, passes, migrancy — defined the era.

questions.question: Closed compounds were used to house and:

questions.question: Migrant labour meant men left rural homes to work in distant mines.
questions.memo: Migrant workers travelled from rural homes to the mines and back.

questions.question: The defeat of African kingdoms made it easier to:

questions.question: The Zulu kingdom was defeated in ____.
questions.memo: The Zulu were defeated in 1879.

questions.question: Land dispossession pushed many men to seek work in the mines.
questions.memo: Losing land forced many African men into migrant mine labour.

questions.question: Closed compounds were 'closed' because workers:
