Lines of ____ run north–south and measure east or west position.
questions.memo: Longitude lines run north–south, measuring east–west position.

questions.question: A smaller scale (like 1:1 000 000) covers a larger area with less detail.
questions.memo: Smaller-scale maps cover larger areas with less detail.

questions.question: To find a town's page and position in an atlas you use the:
questions.memo: The atlas index lists places with their page and grid.

questions.question: A ratio scale of 1:25 000 shows more detail than:
questions.memo: 1:25 000 is larger-scale (more detail) than 1:250 000.

questions.question: Degrees can be divided into smaller units called minutes.
questions.memo: Each degree of latitude or longitude is divided into 60 minutes.

questions.question: Calculating distance between two towns on a map needs the:
questions.memo: You use the map's scale to convert map distance to real distance.

questions.question: A scale written as 1:100 000 is a ____ scale.
questions.memo: 1:100 000 is a ratio (number) scale.

questions.question: Atlases contain maps at world, regional and local scales.
questions.memo: Atlases use a range of scales from world to local.

questions.question: Latitude and longitude together let you give a place's:
questions.memo: Latitude and longitude pinpoint a place's exact location.

SSSP.G8.G1.A2.title: The globe
SSSP.G8.G1.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T1) — Maps & globes: The globe.
SSSP.G8.G1.A2.recovery_strategy: Day/night = spin; seasons = tilt + orbit around the sun.

questions.question: Day and night are caused by the earth:
questions.memo: The earth's daily spin on its axis causes day and night.

questions.question: The seasons are caused by the tilt of the earth's axis as it orbits the sun.
questions.memo: The earth's tilt, combined with its orbit, gives us the seasons.

questions.question: The world is divided into time ____ because different places see the sun at different times.
questions.memo: Time zones account for the sun reaching different longitudes at different times.

questions.question: The earth spins once on its ____ roughly every 24 hours.
questions.memo: One full spin on its axis takes about 24 hours — a day.

questions.question: When it is day on one side of the earth, it is night on the opposite side.
questions.memo: As the earth spins, one side faces the sun (day) while the other faces away (night).

questions.question: An equinox is a time when:
options: Day and night are roughly equal in length
questions.expected: Day and night are roughly equal in length
questions.memo: At an equinox, day and night are about equal everywhere.

questions.question: Which causes the seasons — the earth's spin or its tilt and orbit?
options: Its tilt and orbit around the sun
questions.expected: Its tilt and orbit around the sun
questions.memo: Spin gives day/night; tilt + orbit give the seasons.

questions.question: South Africa has its own standard time.
questions.memo: South African Standard Time is the country's official time zone.

questions.question: Time zones exist because:
options: The Earth spins, so the sun reaches places at different times
questions.expected: The Earth spins, so the sun reaches places at different times
questions.memo: As the Earth spins, the sun reaches different longitudes at different times, so we use time zones.

questions.question: The Earth's tilt causes the seasons as it orbits the sun.
questions.memo: The Earth's tilt, with its orbit, causes the seasons.

questions.question: One full rotation of the Earth on its axis takes about:
questions.memo: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours — a day.

questions.question: The Earth's journey around the sun takes about one ____.
questions.memo: One orbit (revolution) of the sun takes about a year.

questions.question: When it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere, it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
questions.memo: Because of the tilt, the hemispheres have opposite seasons.

questions.question: The international date line is roughly opposite the:
questions.memo: The date line lies roughly opposite the Prime Meridian, near 180°.

questions.question: A solstice is when:
options: Day or night is at its longest
questions.expected: Day or night is at its longest
questions.memo: At a solstice, one hemisphere has its longest day and the other its longest night.

questions.question: The Earth's spin causes day and night.
questions.memo: The daily spin gives us day and night.

questions.question: South African Standard Time is:
options: The official time used in South Africa
questions.expected: The official time used in South Africa
questions.memo: South African Standard Time is the country's official time.

questions.question: The angle of the Earth's ____ helps cause the seasons.
questions.memo: The tilt (angle) of the Earth's axis helps cause the seasons.

questions.question: Different places on Earth can have different times of day at the same moment.
questions.memo: Time zones mean different longitudes have different local times at once.

questions.question: A globe is useful because it shows the Earth's:
questions.memo: A globe shows the Earth's true spherical shape without distortion.

SSSP.G8.G1.A3.title: Satellite images
SSSP.G8.G1.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T1) — Maps & globes: Satellite images.
SSSP.G8.G1.A3.recovery_strategy: Satellite images are photos from space, read by colour and pattern.

questions.question: Satellite images are pictures of the earth taken from:
questions.memo: Satellite images are taken from satellites in space orbiting the earth.

questions.question: Satellite images can show water, vegetation, land use and cloud patterns.
questions.memo: Satellites reveal features like water, plants, land use and clouds.

questions.question: Which of these is a real-world use of satellite images?
questions.memo: Satellite images are used to track weather, land use, disasters and more.

questions.question: Green areas on a satellite image usually show ____.
questions.memo: Green typically marks vegetation; blue water; brown/grey bare land or cities.

questions.question: A tool like Google Earth uses satellite images.
questions.memo: Google Earth displays satellite imagery of the whole planet.

questions.question: Satellite images are useful because they:
options: Show large areas of the earth from above
questions.expected: Show large areas of the earth from above
questions.memo: Satellites give a wide overhead view of large areas, useful for many purposes.

questions.question: Satellites that take images of Earth orbit in:
questions.memo: Imaging satellites orbit Earth in space.

questions.question: Satellite images can help track storms and weather.
questions.memo: Weather satellites track clouds and storms.

questions.question: Blue areas on a satellite image usually show:
questions.memo: Blue usually indicates water on a satellite image.

questions.question: Satellite images can show land ____, such as farms and cities.
questions.memo: Satellite images reveal land use like farms and cities.

questions.question: Satellite images give a view of large areas from above.
questions.memo: Satellites provide a wide overhead view of large areas.

questions.question: Satellite images are useful in disasters because they can show:
options: Floods and damage over a wide area
questions.expected: Floods and damage over a wide area
questions.memo: After disasters, satellites show floods and damage across wide areas.

questions.question: Google Earth is an example of a tool that uses:
questions.memo: Google Earth displays satellite imagery of the planet.

questions.question: Satellite images can show how vegetation changes over time.
questions.memo: Repeated images show how vegetation and land change over time.

questions.question: Compared with a ground photo, a satellite image shows:
questions.memo: Satellite images cover far larger areas than a ground-level photo.

questions.question: Green on a satellite image usually means ____.
questions.memo: Green generally indicates vegetation.

questions.question: Satellite images are never useful for farming.
questions.memo: Farmers use satellite images to monitor crops and land.

questions.question: Satellite images help scientists monitor:
options: The environment and changes on Earth
questions.expected: The environment and changes on Earth
questions.memo: Scientists use satellite images to monitor the environment and change.

SSSP.G8.G2.A1.title: Factors influencing temperature and rainfall
SSSP.G8.G2.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T2) — Climate regions: Factors influencing temperature and rainfall.
SSSP.G8.G2.A1.recovery_strategy: Five controls: latitude, sea, height, currents, mountains.

questions.question: Which factor means places near the equator are generally hotter?
questions.memo: Latitude is a key control: places near the equator receive more direct sun and are hotter.

questions.question: Places at a higher altitude (height) are generally cooler.
questions.memo: Temperature drops as you go higher, so high-altitude places are cooler.

questions.question: Being close to the sea tends to make a place's climate:
questions.memo: The sea moderates temperatures, giving coastal places milder climates.

questions.question: ____ is the height of the land above sea level, and it affects temperature.
questions.memo: Altitude (height above sea level) lowers temperature as it increases.

questions.question: Ocean currents can influence the temperature and rainfall of nearby coasts.
questions.memo: Warm and cold ocean currents affect the temperature and rainfall of coasts.

questions.question: Mountains can affect rainfall by:
options: Forcing air to rise, cool and drop rain
questions.expected: Forcing air to rise, cool and drop rain
questions.memo: Air forced up over mountains cools and releases rain on the windward side (relief rainfall).

questions.question: Sort each factor by what it most directly controls.
questions.expected: Altitude and latitude mainly affect temperature; mountains and currents affect rainfall too.
questions.memo: All five factors shape temperature; mountains and currents strongly shape rainfall as well.

questions.question: As you climb a mountain, the temperature usually:
questions.memo: Temperature falls with altitude, so higher places are cooler.

questions.question: Places far inland often have more extreme temperatures than coastal places.
questions.memo: Inland places have hotter summers and colder winters than the milder coast.

questions.question: The sea affects coastal climate by:
questions.memo: The sea moderates coastal temperatures, making them milder.

questions.question: Distance from the ____ (latitude) affects how hot a place is.
questions.memo: Latitude — distance from the equator — strongly affects temperature.

questions.question: A warm ocean current can make a nearby coast warmer and wetter.
questions.memo: Warm currents can raise temperature and rainfall on nearby coasts.

questions.question: Air forced up over a mountain cools and may produce:
questions.memo: Rising air over mountains cools and can release rain (relief rainfall).

questions.question: A cold ocean current near a coast tends to make it:
questions.memo: Cold currents cool the coast and reduce rainfall.

questions.question: Latitude is the only factor that affects temperature.
questions.memo: Altitude, distance from the sea, currents and mountains all matter too.

questions.question: Highveld areas of South Africa are cooler mainly because of their:
questions.memo: The high-altitude Highveld is cooler because of its height.

questions.question: Height above sea level is called ____.
questions.memo: Altitude is height above sea level.

questions.question: Mountains can create a wetter side and a drier side.
questions.memo: Mountains give a wet windward side and a drier sheltered side.

questions.question: Understanding these factors helps explain why places have:
questions.memo: These factors explain why climates differ from place to place.

SSSP.G8.G2.A2.title: South Africa's climate
SSSP.G8.G2.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T2) — Climate regions: South Africa's climate.
SSSP.G8.G2.A2.recovery_strategy: Compare coastal vs inland, high vs low, east vs west.

questions.question: Why is the coast of Durban generally warmer in winter than inland Johannesburg?
options: Durban is at the coast and lower altitude
Durban is further from the equator
questions.expected: Durban is at the coast and lower altitude
questions.memo: Coastal, low-lying Durban stays milder than high-altitude, inland Johannesburg.

questions.question: South Africa's interior plateau is high in altitude, which keeps it cooler.
questions.memo: The high interior plateau's altitude keeps it cooler than the warm coasts.

questions.question: The west coast of South Africa is influenced by a cold ocean current called the:
questions.memo: The cold Benguela current cools the west coast and keeps it dry.

questions.question: The east coast of South Africa is warmed by the ____ current.
questions.memo: The warm Agulhas current warms the east coast and brings moisture.

questions.question: Different parts of South Africa have different climates.
questions.memo: South Africa has varied climates because the controlling factors differ across the country.

questions.question: Upington, far inland in the west, is known for being:
questions.memo: Inland western places like Upington are hot and dry.

questions.question: Which two factors best explain Cape Town's milder, wetter winters?
options: Coastal location and a winter-rainfall pattern
questions.expected: Coastal location and a winter-rainfall pattern
questions.memo: Cape Town is coastal with a Mediterranean-style winter-rainfall climate.

questions.question: The interior plateau of South Africa is generally:
options: Hot because it is at the coast
questions.memo: The high interior plateau is cooler because of its altitude.

questions.question: Cape Town has a winter-rainfall climate.
questions.memo: Cape Town gets most of its rain in winter (a Mediterranean-type climate).

questions.question: Durban is warm and humid partly because of the:
questions.memo: The warm Agulhas current keeps Durban warm and humid.

questions.question: The west coast is cooled and dried by the cold ____ current.
questions.memo: The cold Benguela current cools and dries the west coast.

questions.question: Most of South Africa receives its rain in summer.
questions.memo: Most of South Africa is a summer-rainfall region (the Cape being an exception).

questions.question: Upington in the west is generally:
questions.memo: Inland western Upington is hot and dry.

questions.question: Why does Johannesburg have cooler temperatures than Durban?
questions.memo: High-altitude inland Johannesburg is cooler than coastal Durban.

questions.question: South Africa has the same climate everywhere.
questions.memo: South Africa has varied climates due to differences in altitude, sea, currents and latitude.

questions.question: Coastal cities tend to have:
questions.memo: The sea keeps coastal cities milder than inland places.

questions.question: The warm ____ current flows down South Africa's east coast.
questions.memo: The warm Agulhas current flows along the east coast.

questions.question: Altitude and ocean currents both help explain South Africa's climates.
questions.memo: Altitude, currents, latitude and distance from the sea shape South Africa's climates.

questions.question: Comparing places like Cape Town and Durban shows that climate depends on:
options: Only the day of the week
questions.memo: Climate at each place results from several factors combined.

SSSP.G8.G2.A3.title: Climate around the world
SSSP.G8.G2.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T2) — Climate regions: Climate around the world.
SSSP.G8.G2.A3.recovery_strategy: Weather = today; climate = the long-run average.

questions.question: What is the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is day-to-day; climate is the long-term average
questions.expected: Weather is day-to-day; climate is the long-term average
questions.memo: Weather is what's happening now; climate is the long-run average pattern.

questions.question: Temperature, humidity, wind and precipitation are all elements of weather.
questions.memo: Weather is described by temperature, humidity, wind and precipitation (rain etc.).

questions.question: A desert climate is mainly:
questions.memo: Deserts are defined by very low rainfall.

questions.question: A ____ climate is mild with wet winters and dry summers, like around the Mediterranean Sea.
questions.memo: Mediterranean climates have mild, wet winters and warm, dry summers.

questions.question: Use the climate data. Station X: warmest month 26°C, coldest 24°C, rain every month. Which climate type?
questions.memo: Hot all year with high rainfall every month points to a tropical climate.

questions.question: Climate regions of the world can be shown on a map.
questions.memo: World climate maps show where different climate types occur.

questions.question: A polar climate is:
questions.memo: Polar climates near the poles are extremely cold.

questions.question: Bar and line graphs are commonly used to show a place's:
questions.memo: Climate graphs use bars for rainfall and a line for temperature.

questions.question: Weather describes conditions:
questions.memo: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere.

questions.question: Climate is the average weather of a place over many years.
questions.memo: Climate is the long-term average of weather.

questions.question: A tropical climate is:
questions.memo: Tropical climates are hot with high rainfall.

questions.question: A ____ climate has very low rainfall.
questions.memo: Desert climates are very dry.

questions.question: Polar climates are found near the North and South Poles.
questions.memo: Polar climates occur near the poles and are very cold.

questions.question: Humidity is a measure of:
questions.memo: Humidity measures how much moisture is in the air.

questions.question: Climate graphs usually show rainfall as bars and temperature as a:
questions.memo: Climate graphs use rainfall bars and a temperature line.

questions.question: A temperate climate is mild, without extreme heat or cold.
questions.memo: Temperate climates are mild, avoiding extremes.

questions.question: Climate regions can be linked to the factors that control:
questions.memo: Climate regions follow the factors controlling temperature and rainfall.

questions.question: The elements of weather include temperature, wind, humidity and ____.
questions.memo: Precipitation (rain, snow) is an element of weather.

questions.question: A world climate map shows where different climate types occur.
questions.memo: World climate maps display the locations of climate types.

questions.question: The difference between weather and climate is mainly about:
questions.memo: Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average.

SSSP.G8.G3.A1.title: Settlement and land use
SSSP.G8.G3.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T3) — Settlement & urbanisation: Settlement and land use.
SSSP.G8.G3.A1.recovery_strategy: A city has zones: business centre, industry, and where people live.

questions.question: The central business district (CBD) of a city is mainly used for:
questions.memo: The CBD is the city's centre of shops, offices and business.

questions.question: Urban settlements have different land-use zones, such as residential and industrial areas.
questions.memo: Cities are divided into zones: business, industry, residential and recreation.

questions.question: Which is an example of a rural settlement type?
questions.memo: Rural settlements include farming, mining, forestry and fishing communities.

questions.question: Areas of a city where people live are called ____ areas.
questions.memo: Residential areas are where people live, ranging from high- to low-income.

questions.question: Heavy industry is usually placed in the middle of residential suburbs.
questions.memo: Heavy industry is usually zoned away from homes, often on the city's edge.

questions.question: Mining, forestry and fishing settlements are examples of:
questions.memo: These resource-based settlements are types of rural settlement.

questions.question: Why do cities separate land into zones?
questions.memo: Zoning organises a city so different activities (homes, work, industry) fit together.

questions.question: A 'settlement' is:
questions.memo: A settlement is a place where people live, from a village to a city.

questions.question: Light and heavy industry are usually placed in separate zones.
questions.memo: Cities zone light and heavy industry separately, often away from homes.

questions.question: Recreation areas in a city are for:
questions.memo: Recreation zones provide for sport and leisure.

questions.question: The busy commercial centre of a city is the ____.
questions.memo: The central business district (CBD) is the city's commercial centre.

questions.question: Forestry and fishing settlements are types of rural settlement.
questions.memo: Rural settlements include farming, mining, forestry and fishing communities.

questions.question: Residential areas can be:
questions.memo: Residential zones range from high- to low-income areas.

questions.question: Zoning a city helps to:
questions.memo: Zoning organises activities so they fit together better.

questions.question: All settlements are the same size and type.
questions.memo: Settlements vary from tiny villages to huge cities, urban and rural.

questions.question: A mining town is an example of a:
options: Rural settlement based on a resource
questions.expected: Rural settlement based on a resource
questions.memo: Mining towns are resource-based rural settlements.

questions.question: Areas where people live are called ____ areas.
questions.memo: Residential areas are where people live.

questions.question: Land use describes how an area of land is used.
questions.memo: Land use is what an area of land is used for (homes, shops, industry, etc.).

questions.question: Heavy industry is often placed on the city's edge to:
options: Keep pollution and noise away from homes
questions.expected: Keep pollution and noise away from homes
questions.memo: Heavy industry is zoned away from homes to reduce pollution and noise nuisance.

SSSP.G8.G3.A2.title: Land use on aerial photographs
SSSP.G8.G3.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T3) — Settlement & urbanisation: Land use on aerial photographs.
SSSP.G8.G3.A2.recovery_strategy: Vertical photo = straight down (like a map); oblique = at an angle.

questions.question: A vertical aerial photograph is taken:
options: At an angle from the side
questions.memo: Vertical aerial photos look straight down, like a map view.

questions.question: An oblique aerial photograph is taken at an angle and shows the sides of features.
questions.memo: Oblique photos are taken at an angle, showing features' sides, like a bird's-eye view.

questions.question: Aerial photographs are useful for identifying:
options: Land use and features from above
questions.expected: Land use and features from above
questions.memo: Aerial photos help identify natural and built features and land use from above.

questions.question: A photo taken straight down from above is a ____ aerial photograph.
questions.memo: Straight-down = vertical; angled = oblique.

questions.question: Aerial photographs can show both natural features (like rivers) and constructed features (like roads).
questions.memo: Aerial photos reveal natural features and human-made (constructed) features alike.

questions.question: Which would be easier to identify on a vertical aerial photo of a town?
options: The pattern of streets and buildings
questions.expected: The pattern of streets and buildings
questions.memo: Overhead photos clearly show the layout of streets and buildings.

questions.question: A vertical aerial photo looks like a:
questions.memo: Vertical aerial photos give a straight-down, map-like view.

questions.question: Oblique aerial photos are taken at an angle.
questions.memo: Oblique photos are taken at an angle, showing the sides of features.

questions.question: Aerial photographs can show:
questions.memo: Aerial photos reveal natural and built (constructed) features.

questions.question: A straight-down aerial photo is a ____ photo.
questions.memo: A straight-down photo is vertical.

questions.question: Aerial photos help identify land use in a settlement.
questions.memo: Aerial photos help you see and identify land use in settlements.

questions.question: Which would be easiest to spot on an aerial photo of a city?
questions.memo: Roads and building patterns are clearly visible from above.

questions.question: An oblique photo is useful because it shows:
options: The sides and shapes of features
questions.expected: The sides and shapes of features
questions.memo: Oblique photos show the sides and 3D shapes of features.

questions.question: A river is a natural feature visible on an aerial photo.
questions.memo: Rivers are natural features clearly seen on aerial photos.

questions.question: Land-use maps often use:
options: Shading and colours for different zones
questions.expected: Shading and colours for different zones
questions.memo: Shaded land-use maps show different zones by colour.

questions.question: A road is a ____ (human-made) feature on an aerial photo.
questions.memo: Roads are constructed (human-made) features.

questions.question: Aerial photos can only be taken from straight above.
questions.memo: Aerial photos can be vertical (straight down) or oblique (at an angle).

questions.question: Comparing an aerial photo with a map helps you:
questions.memo: Combining photo and map gives a fuller understanding of an area.

SSSP.G8.G3.A3.title: Urbanisation
SSSP.G8.G3.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T3) — Settlement & urbanisation: Urbanisation.
SSSP.G8.G3.A3.recovery_strategy: Push = reasons to leave the country; pull = reasons cities attract people.

questions.question: Urbanisation is the process of:
options: People moving to and cities growing
questions.expected: People moving to and cities growing
questions.memo: Urbanisation is the growth of cities as people move from rural areas.

questions.question: 'Pull factors' are things that attract people to cities, like jobs.
questions.memo: Pull factors (jobs, services) draw people toward cities.

questions.question: A 'push factor' driving people from rural areas could be:
options: Lack of jobs or land in the countryside
questions.expected: Lack of jobs or land in the countryside
questions.memo: Push factors (poverty, no land, no work) drive people away from rural areas.

questions.question: Things that attract people to the city are ____ factors.
questions.memo: Pull factors attract; push factors drive away.

questions.question: Sort each reason for moving as a PUSH (from the countryside) or PULL (toward the city) factor.

items.text: More job opportunities in the city

questions.expected: No jobs and drought push people away; hospitals and jobs pull them to the city.
questions.memo: Push factors drive people out of rural areas; pull factors attract them to cities.

questions.question: A social issue caused by rapid city growth is:
questions.memo: Rapid urban growth strains housing, water, health care and other services.

questions.question: Apartheid laws controlled where black South Africans could live and move.
questions.memo: Apartheid population controls restricted black South Africans' movement and residence, shaping urbanisation.

questions.question: Urbanisation means the growth of:
questions.memo: Urbanisation is the growth of cities as people move in.

questions.question: A drought that ruins crops is a push factor driving people to cities.
questions.memo: Drought and crop failure push people from rural areas to cities.

questions.question: Better jobs and services in a city are examples of:
questions.memo: Jobs and services pull people toward the city.

questions.question: Reasons that drive people away from rural areas are ____ factors.
questions.memo: Push factors drive people away from rural areas.

questions.question: Rapid city growth can lead to a shortage of housing and services.
questions.memo: Fast urban growth strains housing, water, health care and other services.

questions.question: Apartheid laws affected urbanisation by:
options: Controlling where black South Africans could live
questions.expected: Controlling where black South Africans could live
questions.memo: Apartheid population controls restricted black South Africans' movement and residence.

questions.question: Informal settlements often grow because:
options: People move to cities faster than housing is built
questions.expected: People move to cities faster than housing is built
questions.memo: When migration outpaces housing, informal settlements grow.

questions.question: Urbanisation only happens in South Africa.
questions.memo: Urbanisation happens across the world, not only in South Africa.

questions.question: A pull factor for cities is:
questions.memo: Better health care is a pull factor attracting people to cities.

questions.question: The fast growth of cities can strain ____ provision like water and housing.
questions.memo: Rapid growth strains the provision of services like water and housing.

questions.question: Migration to cities is driven by both push and pull factors.
questions.memo: People move because of push factors (rural problems) and pull factors (city attractions).

questions.question: A social issue linked to urbanisation is:
options: Access to housing and health care
questions.expected: Access to housing and health care
questions.memo: Urbanisation raises social issues like housing and health-care access.

SSSP.G8.G4.A1.title: Trade and transport around the world
SSSP.G8.G4.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G8 T4) — Transport & trade: Trade and transport around the world.
SSSP.G8.G4.A1.recovery_strategy: Trade needs transport — match the goods to the best mode.

questions.question: People trade mainly because:
options: Different places have different goods and needs
Everyone has exactly the same things
questions.expected: Different places have different goods and needs
questions.memo: Trade lets places exchange what they have for what they need.

questions.question: Trade and transport are closely linked: goods must be moved to be traded.
questions.memo: Transport carries traded goods between places, so trade depends on transport.

questions.question: Which mode of transport is best for carrying heavy goods across oceans?
questions.memo: Ships carry large, heavy loads across oceans cheaply, ideal for bulky goods.

questions.question: Oil and gas are often moved long distances through a ____.
questions.memo: Pipelines efficiently move liquids and gases like oil over long distances.

questions.question: Air transport is the fastest way to move goods over long distances.
questions.memo: Air transport is fastest but more expensive, good for urgent or light goods.

questions.question: Sort each cargo with the most suitable transport mode.

items.text: Thousands of tonnes of coal across an ocean
Urgent medicine to another country fast
Crude oil from the coast to a refinery inland

questions.expected: Bulk coal by sea, urgent medicine by air, oil by pipeline.
questions.memo: Match the cargo to the mode: bulky → sea, urgent/light → air, liquid → pipeline.

questions.question: Which are the five main modes of transport in this topic?
options: Sea, air, road, rail and pipeline
questions.expected: Sea, air, road, rail and pipeline
questions.memo: The main modes are sea, air, road, rail and pipeline.

questions.question: Rail transport is well suited to carrying:
questions.memo: Rail efficiently moves heavy goods overland.

questions.question: Road transport is flexible and can deliver door to door.
questions.memo: Road transport is flexible, reaching destinations directly.

questions.question: Trade happens because places have:
questions.memo: Trade lets places exchange what they have for what they need.

questions.question: Liquids like oil are best moved by ____.
questions.memo: Pipelines efficiently move liquids like oil.

SSSP.G9.G1.A4.title: Interpreting maps and photographs
SSSP.G9.G1.A4.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T1) — Map skills (topographic & orthophoto): Interpreting maps and photographs.
SSSP.G9.G1.A4.recovery_strategy: Combine sources: the map gives height, the photo gives detail.

questions.question: Cross-referencing a map and an aerial photo of the same area helps you to:
questions.memo: Using a map and photo together gives a fuller, cross-checked understanding of an area.

questions.question: Settlement patterns (shape, size, location) can be identified from maps and photos.
questions.memo: Maps and photos let you describe a settlement's shape, size and location.

questions.question: Describing the 'landscape' from a map means describing:
options: The shape and features of the land
questions.expected: The shape and features of the land
questions.memo: Describing the landscape means the land's shape, height and features.

questions.question: How land is used — for farming, housing or industry — is called land ____.
questions.memo: Land use describes what an area of land is used for.

questions.question: A topographic map and an aerial photo must always be of exactly the same area to be useful together.
questions.memo: It helps but isn't essential — comparing an area shown in different ways is still very worthwhile.

questions.question: Identifying whether a settlement is large or small from a map is describing its:
questions.memo: Size is one feature of a settlement you can read from a map or photo.

questions.question: Describing a 'settlement pattern' means describing its:
questions.memo: Settlement pattern covers the shape, size and location of a settlement.

questions.question: A map shows height well, while a photo shows real detail well.
questions.memo: Maps show height (contours); photos show real detail — they complement each other.

questions.question: Cross-referencing sources means:
options: Comparing information from more than one source
questions.expected: Comparing information from more than one source
questions.memo: Cross-referencing compares information across sources.

questions.question: Whether land is used for farming or housing is its land ____.
questions.memo: Land use is how an area of land is used.

questions.question: Maps and photos of the same area must always match exactly to be useful.
questions.memo: It helps but isn't essential — comparing an area shown different ways is still worthwhile.

questions.question: A large settlement spread out along a road has a settlement shape that is:
questions.memo: A settlement strung along a road has a linear shape.

questions.question: Combining a map and a photo helps you:
options: Build a fuller picture of the area
questions.expected: Build a fuller picture of the area
questions.memo: Together they give a fuller, cross-checked picture of the area.

questions.question: You can identify land use from both maps and photographs.
questions.memo: Both maps and photos can reveal how land is used.

questions.question: Describing the 'landscape' means describing the land's:
questions.memo: Landscape description covers the land's shape and features.

questions.question: A settlement's ____ tells you whether it is large or small.
questions.memo: Size tells you how large or small a settlement is.

questions.question: Interpreting maps and photos is an important geographical skill.
questions.memo: Reading and comparing maps and photos is a key geographical skill.

questions.question: Why use several sources together?
questions.memo: Different sources reveal different information, giving a fuller understanding.

SSSP.G9.G2.A1.title: Meaning and measuring development
SSSP.G9.G2.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T2) — Development issues: Meaning and measuring development.
SSSP.G9.G2.A1.recovery_strategy: HDI blends income, education and life expectancy into one score.

questions.question: 'Development' is about improving people's:
questions.memo: Development means improving quality of life — economic, social and environmental well-being.

questions.question: The Human Development Index (HDI) measures development using more than just income.
questions.memo: The HDI combines life expectancy, education and income — not income alone.

questions.question: Which three things does the HDI combine?
questions.memo: HDI blends life expectancy, education and per-capita income into one score.

questions.question: A country with a high HDI generally has good health, education and ____.
questions.memo: High-HDI countries score well on health, education and income.

questions.question: Use the data. Which country has the highest HDI? A: 0.92, B: 0.55, C: 0.70.
questions.memo: HDI runs from 0 to 1; the highest value (0.92) is Country A — the most developed.

questions.question: Development includes economic, social and environmental aspects.
questions.memo: True development balances economic, social and environmental well-being.

questions.question: A country ranked 'low development' on a world HDI map usually has:
options: Lower income, health and education levels
questions.expected: Lower income, health and education levels
questions.memo: Low-development countries tend to have lower income, health and education.

questions.question: A more developed country usually has:
questions.memo: More developed countries tend to have higher income, health and education.

questions.question: The HDI gives a score between 0 and 1.
questions.memo: The HDI ranges from 0 (low) to 1 (high development).

questions.question: Life expectancy is part of the HDI because it reflects:
questions.memo: Life expectancy reflects a population's health, part of the HDI.

questions.question: The Human Development ____ measures development.
questions.memo: The Human Development Index (HDI) measures development.

questions.question: Development is only about money.
questions.memo: Development includes health, education and well-being, not just money.

questions.question: Education is part of the HDI because it reflects:
options: Knowledge and skills in a population
questions.expected: Knowledge and skills in a population
questions.memo: Education levels reflect a population's knowledge and skills.

questions.question: A country with HDI of 0.40 is generally:
questions.memo: An HDI of 0.40 indicates lower development.

questions.question: Comparing HDI scores helps rank countries by development.
questions.memo: HDI scores let us compare and rank countries' development.

questions.question: Development also has an ____ side, like protecting the environment.
questions.memo: True development includes an environmental dimension.

questions.question: The HDI combines income, education and ____.
questions.memo: HDI blends income, education and life expectancy.

questions.question: A high life expectancy usually goes with good health care.
questions.memo: Good health care tends to raise life expectancy.

questions.question: Why measure development with more than just income?
options: A fuller picture of people's well-being
questions.expected: A fuller picture of people's well-being
questions.memo: Using health and education too gives a fuller picture of well-being.

SSSP.G9.G2.A2.title: Factors affecting development
SSSP.G9.G2.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T2) — Development issues: Factors affecting development.
SSSP.G9.G2.A2.recovery_strategy: No single cause — development comes from many factors together.

questions.question: Which historical factor helps explain why some countries are less developed?
questions.memo: Colonialism is a key historical factor shaping today's development differences.

questions.question: Unfair trade can keep some countries poorer than others.
questions.memo: Unequal, unfair trade relationships can hold back a country's development.

questions.question: Which factor generally HELPS a country to develop?
questions.memo: Strong education and health support development; war and instability hold it back.

questions.question: Political ____ — a stable, peaceful government — supports development.
questions.memo: Political stability gives the security needed for development.

questions.question: Sort each factor by whether it usually HELPS or HARMS development.
questions.expected: Education, health and stability help; war and unfair trade harm development.
questions.memo: Health, education and stability build development; conflict and unfair trade undermine it.

questions.question: Technology and industrialisation can affect a country's level of development.
questions.memo: Access to technology and industry is an important factor in development.

questions.question: There is no single cause of development differences because:
questions.memo: Development differences come from many interacting factors, not one cause.

questions.question: Colonialism affected development by:
questions.memo: Colonial economies were shaped to serve the colonisers, affecting later development.

questions.question: Good education and health care support a country's development.
questions.memo: Strong education and health care help development.

questions.question: Political instability tends to:
questions.memo: Instability and conflict hold back development.

questions.question: Unfair ____ can keep some countries poorer.
questions.memo: Unfair trade can keep countries poorer.

questions.question: Technology and industry can boost a country's development.
questions.memo: Access to technology and industry can boost development.

questions.question: There is usually no single cause of underdevelopment because:
questions.memo: Underdevelopment comes from many interacting factors.

questions.question: Better health care helps development by:
questions.memo: Healthy people are more productive, aiding development.

questions.question: History, like colonialism, can still affect development today.
questions.memo: Historical factors like colonialism continue to shape development.

questions.question: War harms development because it:
questions.memo: War destroys lives, infrastructure and stability, harming development.

questions.question: Political ____ provides the security needed for development.
questions.memo: Political stability provides security for development.

questions.question: All countries developed in exactly the same way.
questions.memo: Countries developed differently because of different histories and factors.

questions.question: Understanding the factors helps us see development as:
questions.memo: Development is complex, shaped by many causes.

SSSP.G9.G2.A3.title: Opportunities for development
SSSP.G9.G2.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T2) — Development issues: Opportunities for development.
SSSP.G9.G2.A3.recovery_strategy: Development should also be fair and sustainable, not just bigger.

questions.question: 'Fairer trade' would help development by:
options: Giving poorer countries better prices for their goods
questions.expected: Giving poorer countries better prices for their goods
questions.memo: More equal trade gives developing countries fairer prices and a better chance to grow.

questions.question: Sustainable development meets today's needs without harming future generations.
questions.memo: Sustainable development balances today's needs with the needs of the future.

questions.question: 'Alternative development' suggests that countries:
options: Do not all have to copy heavy industrialisation
questions.expected: Do not all have to copy heavy industrialisation
questions.memo: Alternative development looks for paths beyond just heavy industrialisation.

questions.question: Development that lasts and protects the future is called ____ development.
questions.memo: Sustainable development is development that can continue without harming the future.

questions.question: Community-based projects can be one way to support development.
questions.memo: Local, community-based projects are one approach to improving development.

questions.question: Why think critically about 'development'?
options: It should improve quality of life and care for the poor and planet
It is always good no matter what
questions.expected: It should improve quality of life and care for the poor and planet
questions.memo: A critical view asks whether development truly improves lives and respects the planet.

questions.question: Fairer trade helps poorer countries by giving them:
questions.memo: Fairer trade gives developing countries better prices for their goods.

questions.question: Sustainable development tries not to harm future generations.
questions.memo: Sustainable development meets today's needs without harming the future.

questions.question: Alternative development means countries can:
options: Follow paths other than heavy industrialisation
questions.expected: Follow paths other than heavy industrialisation
questions.memo: Alternative development explores paths beyond heavy industrialisation.

questions.question: Development that lasts and protects the future is ____ development.
questions.memo: Sustainable development can continue without harming the future.

questions.question: Community-based projects can support local development.
questions.memo: Local, community-based projects are one route to development.

questions.question: A critical view of development asks whether it truly:
options: Improves quality of life and respects the planet
questions.expected: Improves quality of life and respects the planet
questions.memo: A critical view asks if development really improves lives and respects the planet.

questions.question: Education and training programmes help development by:
questions.memo: Education and training build the skills a country needs to develop.

questions.question: More equal trade relationships can create development opportunities.
questions.memo: Fairer trade creates opportunities for development.

questions.question: Sustainable development balances economic, social and:
questions.memo: Sustainable development balances economic, social and environmental needs.

questions.question: Rural ____ programmes can improve life in the countryside.
questions.memo: Rural development programmes improve life in rural areas.

questions.question: There is only one way for every country to develop.
questions.memo: Countries can develop in different ways suited to their situations.

questions.question: Opportunities for development include:
options: Fair trade, sustainability and community projects
questions.expected: Fair trade, sustainability and community projects
questions.memo: Fairer trade, sustainability and community projects are development opportunities.

SSSP.G9.G3.A1.title: Weathering
SSSP.G9.G3.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T3) — Surface forces that shape the earth: Weathering.
SSSP.G9.G3.A1.caps_topic: Surface forces that shape the earth
SSSP.G9.G3.A1.recovery_strategy: Weathering breaks rock in place; it doesn't move it (that's erosion).

questions.question: Weathering is the process that:
options: Breaks down rock where it is
questions.expected: Breaks down rock where it is
questions.memo: Weathering breaks rock down in place; it does not move it (that's erosion).

questions.question: Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of.
questions.memo: Physical weathering breaks rock apart mechanically, without changing its chemistry.

questions.question: Chemical weathering changes rock by:
options: Reacting with water or acids to change its minerals
questions.expected: Reacting with water or acids to change its minerals
questions.memo: Chemical weathering alters the minerals in rock through reactions with water or acids.

questions.question: When plant roots grow into and break apart rock, this is ____ weathering.
questions.memo: Biological weathering involves living things, like roots, breaking rock.

questions.question: Human activities can speed up weathering.
questions.memo: Activities like mining and pollution can increase the rate of weathering.

questions.question: Sort each example into the correct type of weathering.

items.text: Water freezes in a crack and splits the rock
Tree roots break apart a rock

questions.expected: Freezing = physical, acid = chemical, roots = biological.
questions.memo: Physical = mechanical breaking; chemical = changing minerals; biological = living things.

questions.question: Which is an example of physical weathering?
options: Water freezing and thawing in cracks
questions.expected: Water freezing and thawing in cracks
questions.memo: Freeze-thaw is a classic example of physical weathering.

questions.question: Weathering breaks down rock:
options: Where it is, without moving it
questions.expected: Where it is, without moving it
questions.memo: Weathering breaks rock in place; moving it is erosion.

questions.question: Freeze-thaw is a kind of physical weathering.
questions.memo: Water freezing and thawing in cracks (freeze-thaw) is physical weathering.

questions.question: Acid rain dissolving rock is an example of:
questions.memo: Acid reacting with rock is chemical weathering.

questions.question: Tree roots breaking rock apart is ____ weathering.
questions.memo: Living things breaking rock is biological weathering.

questions.question: Mining and pollution can speed up weathering.
questions.memo: Human activities like mining and pollution can speed up weathering.

questions.question: Physical weathering changes rock by:
questions.memo: Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry.

questions.question: Chemical weathering changes the rock's:
questions.memo: Chemical weathering changes the minerals that make up the rock.

questions.question: Weathering and erosion are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion moves it — they are different.

questions.question: Rust forming on rock containing iron is an example of:
questions.memo: Rusting (oxidation) is a chemical weathering process.

questions.question: Weathering breaks rock ____ it is, without moving it.
questions.memo: Weathering breaks rock where it is.

questions.question: Plants and animals can cause biological weathering.
questions.memo: Living things, like roots and burrowing animals, cause biological weathering.

questions.question: Why is weathering important?
options: It helps form soil and shape landscapes
questions.expected: It helps form soil and shape landscapes
questions.memo: Weathering helps form soil and shape the landscape over time.

SSSP.G9.G3.A2.title: Erosion and deposition
SSSP.G9.G3.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T3) — Surface forces that shape the earth: Erosion and deposition.
SSSP.G9.G3.A2.caps_topic: Surface forces that shape the earth
SSSP.G9.G3.A2.recovery_strategy: Erosion carries material away; deposition drops it somewhere else.

questions.question: Erosion is different from weathering because erosion:
questions.memo: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion carries the loosened material away.

questions.question: Rivers, the sea, wind and ice can all cause erosion.
questions.memo: Moving water, waves, wind and ice are all agents of erosion.

questions.question: Deposition happens when:
options: Material that was carried is dropped in a new place
questions.expected: Material that was carried is dropped in a new place
questions.memo: Deposition is the dropping of eroded material in a new location.

questions.question: A river drops sand and mud, building up a flat fertile area at its mouth called a ____.
questions.memo: A delta is land built by river deposition at the mouth of a river.

questions.question: Wind can both erode and deposit material, for example forming sand dunes.
questions.memo: Wind erodes loose material and deposits it elsewhere, building features like dunes.

questions.question: Sort each as an example of EROSION or DEPOSITION.

items.text: A river drops sand to form a delta
Wind blows soil off a bare field

questions.expected: Wearing away = erosion; dropping/building up = deposition.
questions.memo: Erosion wears away and carries off; deposition drops material to build new features.

questions.question: Moving ice (a glacier) shapes the land by:
options: Eroding and depositing material as it moves
questions.expected: Eroding and depositing material as it moves
questions.memo: Glaciers erode the land they pass over and deposit material as they melt.

questions.question: Erosion is the process of:
options: Wearing away and carrying off material
questions.expected: Wearing away and carrying off material
questions.memo: Erosion wears away and transports material; weathering just breaks it in place.

questions.question: A river can both erode and deposit material along its course.
questions.memo: Rivers erode in some places and deposit material in others.

questions.question: Waves wearing away a cliff is an example of:
questions.memo: Waves wearing away a cliff is erosion by the sea.

questions.question: Material dropped by a river at its mouth can form a ____.
questions.memo: A delta forms from river deposition at the mouth.

questions.question: Wind can shape the land by erosion and deposition.
questions.memo: Wind erodes loose material and deposits it, e.g. as dunes.

questions.question: Glaciers (moving ice) shape land by:
questions.memo: Glaciers erode the land and deposit material as they move and melt.

questions.question: Deposition is when carried material is:
questions.memo: Deposition drops carried material in a new place.

questions.question: Sand dunes are formed by wind deposition.
questions.memo: Wind deposits sand to build dunes.

questions.question: Which agent of erosion is most important in a desert?
questions.memo: In dry deserts, wind is a major agent of erosion and deposition.

questions.question: Rivers, sea, ice and ____ are all agents of erosion.
questions.memo: Wind, along with rivers, sea and ice, erodes the land.

questions.question: Erosion and deposition together reshape the Earth's surface over time.
questions.memo: Erosion and deposition continually reshape landscapes over time.

questions.question: The difference between erosion and weathering is that erosion:
options: Moves material; weathering breaks it in place
questions.expected: Moves material; weathering breaks it in place
questions.memo: Erosion transports material; weathering breaks it where it is.

SSSP.G9.G3.A3.title: People and soil erosion
SSSP.G9.G3.A3.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T3) — Surface forces that shape the earth: People and soil erosion.
SSSP.G9.G3.A3.caps_topic: Surface forces that shape the earth
SSSP.G9.G3.A3.recovery_strategy: Bare, overworked soil washes or blows away fastest.

questions.question: Which human activity is a major cause of soil erosion?
questions.memo: Poor farming, construction and mining strip and loosen soil, causing erosion.

questions.question: Removing vegetation makes soil erosion worse.
questions.memo: Plants hold soil together; removing them lets soil wash or blow away more easily.

questions.question: Overgrazing by too many animals causes soil erosion because it:
options: Strips away the plants that protect the soil
questions.expected: Strips away the plants that protect the soil
questions.memo: Overgrazing removes the protective plant cover, exposing soil to erosion.

questions.question: When fertile topsoil is washed or blown away, farmland loses its ____.
questions.memo: Losing topsoil means losing fertility, which harms farming.

questions.question: Soil erosion can reduce the amount of food a region can produce.
questions.memo: Eroded, less fertile soil produces less food, threatening food supply.

questions.question: Which practice would help REDUCE soil erosion on farmland?
options: Ploughing straight down a steep slope
questions.memo: Cover crops, trees and careful methods protect soil and reduce erosion.

questions.question: Construction and mining can also contribute to soil erosion.
questions.memo: Clearing land for construction and mining exposes soil and adds to erosion.

questions.question: Soil erosion is harmful because it:
options: Removes fertile topsoil needed for farming
questions.expected: Removes fertile topsoil needed for farming
questions.memo: Erosion strips fertile topsoil, harming farming.

questions.question: Overgrazing removes the plants that protect the soil.
questions.memo: Too many animals strip plant cover, exposing soil to erosion.

questions.question: Ploughing straight down a steep slope can:
questions.memo: Ploughing down a slope lets water run fast and erode soil.

questions.question: Plant ____ helps hold soil in place and reduce erosion.
questions.memo: Plant cover holds soil and reduces erosion.

questions.question: Construction and mining can cause soil erosion.
questions.memo: Clearing land for construction and mining exposes soil to erosion.

questions.question: One way to reduce soil erosion on a slope is:
options: Planting along the contour or terracing
questions.expected: Planting along the contour or terracing
questions.memo: Contour planting and terracing slow water and reduce erosion.

questions.question: Soil erosion can reduce a region's:
questions.memo: Eroded soil grows less food, threatening food supply.

questions.question: Wind can also cause soil erosion on bare land.
questions.memo: Wind blows away soil from bare, dry land.

questions.question: Trees help reduce soil erosion because their roots:
questions.memo: Tree roots bind the soil, reducing erosion.

questions.question: Putting too many animals on land causes ____.
questions.memo: Too many animals on the land causes overgrazing and erosion.

questions.question: People can both cause and reduce soil erosion.
questions.memo: Human actions can cause erosion or, with care, reduce it.

questions.question: A case study of agriculture and erosion shows that farming can:
questions.memo: Poor farming can damage soil through erosion.

SSSP.G9.G4.A1.title: Resource use
SSSP.G9.G4.A1.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T4) — Resource use & sustainability: Resource use.
SSSP.G9.G4.A1.recovery_strategy: Renewable can refill if used carefully; non-renewable runs out.

questions.question: A renewable resource is one that:
options: Can be replaced or refilled if used carefully
Can never run out no matter what
questions.expected: Can be replaced or refilled if used carefully
questions.memo: Renewable resources (like forests, fish) can recover if used carefully.

questions.question: Coal and oil are non-renewable resources.
questions.memo: Coal and oil take millions of years to form, so they are non-renewable.

questions.question: Over-fishing the oceans is a problem because it:
options: Uses fish faster than they can breed and recover
questions.expected: Uses fish faster than they can breed and recover
questions.memo: Over-fishing takes fish faster than they can reproduce, depleting the resource.

questions.question: Resources that run out and cannot be replaced are called ____ resources.
questions.memo: Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once used up.

questions.question: Sort each resource as renewable or non-renewable.
questions.expected: Sun and wind are renewable; coal and oil are non-renewable.
questions.memo: Renewable sources (sun, wind) refill naturally; fossil fuels (coal, oil) do not.

questions.question: Overgrazing land is an example of unwise resource use.
questions.memo: Overgrazing damages the land, an example of using a resource unwisely.

questions.question: Why should non-renewable resources be used carefully?
options: Once used up they cannot be replaced
questions.expected: Once used up they cannot be replaced
questions.memo: Non-renewables are finite, so careful use makes them last longer.

questions.question: Solar and wind energy are examples of:
questions.memo: Sun and wind are renewable — they don't run out.

questions.question: Fossil fuels like coal and oil are non-renewable.
questions.memo: Coal and oil take millions of years to form and cannot be quickly replaced.

questions.question: Over-grazing damages land by:
questions.memo: Over-grazing strips plant cover, damaging the land.

questions.question: Resources that can be replaced if used carefully are ____.
questions.memo: Renewable resources can be replaced if used carefully.

questions.question: Over-fishing can collapse fish populations.
questions.memo: Catching fish faster than they breed can collapse their populations.

questions.question: Why should non-renewable resources be used carefully?
options: They cannot be replaced once used up
questions.expected: They cannot be replaced once used up
questions.memo: Non-renewables are finite, so careful use matters.

questions.question: Water can be a renewable resource if it is:
questions.memo: Water can renew if used and managed carefully, but can be over-used or polluted.

questions.question: Unwise use of resources can harm the environment.
questions.memo: Using resources unwisely damages the environment.

questions.question: Coal is used mainly to:
questions.memo: Coal is burned mainly to produce energy.

questions.question: Once used up, ____ resources cannot be replaced.
questions.memo: Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced once used up.

questions.question: Renewable resources can still be damaged if used carelessly.
questions.memo: Even renewable resources (like fish or water) can be harmed by careless use.

questions.question: The effects of unwise resource use include:
questions.memo: Over-fishing and over-grazing are effects of unwise resource use.

SSSP.G9.G4.A2.title: Sustainable use of resources
SSSP.G9.G4.A2.description: Geography (CAPS G9 T4) — Resource use & sustainability: Sustainable use of resources.
SSSP.G9.G4.A2.recovery_strategy: Sustainable = meeting today's needs without robbing the future.

questions.question: Sustainable use of a resource means using it:
options: So it can keep being available in the future
questions.expected: So it can keep being available in the future
questions.memo: Sustainable use keeps a resource available for the future.

questions.question: Sustainable fishing means catching fish at a rate they can replace.
questions.memo: Sustainable fishing keeps catches within the level fish can naturally replace.

questions.question: Who has a role in choosing more sustainable resource use?
questions.memo: Everyone — individuals, businesses and governments — can choose more sustainable use.

questions.question: Reducing the amount of carbon we release helps lower our carbon ____.
questions.memo: Your 'carbon footprint' is the amount of carbon your activities release.

questions.question: Sustainable land use for grazing means not putting too many animals on the land.
questions.memo: Limiting animal numbers prevents overgrazing, keeping grazing land sustainable.

questions.question: Which choice helps reduce pressure on resources?
questions.memo: Reduce, reuse and recycle all lower the pressure on resources.

questions.question: Sustainability is only about the environment and never about people or the economy.
questions.memo: Sustainability balances environmental, social and economic needs together.

questions.question: Sustainable use means using resources so they:
questions.memo: Sustainable use keeps resources available for the future.

questions.question: Recycling helps reduce pressure on resources.
questions.memo: Recycling reuses materials, reducing pressure on resources.

questions.question: Sustainable fishing means catching fish:
options: At a rate they can replace
questions.expected: At a rate they can replace
questions.memo: Sustainable fishing keeps catches within the rate fish can replace.

questions.question: 'Reduce, reuse and ____' is a guide to sustainable living.
questions.memo: Reduce, reuse and recycle guide sustainable living.

questions.question: Governments, businesses and individuals all have a role in sustainability.
questions.memo: Everyone — governments, businesses and individuals — can choose sustainable use.

questions.question: Lowering your carbon footprint means:
options: Releasing less carbon through your choices
questions.expected: Releasing less carbon through your choices
questions.memo: A lower carbon footprint means choices that release less carbon.

questions.question: Sustainable grazing means:
options: Not putting too many animals on the land
Adding as many animals as possible
questions.expected: Not putting too many animals on the land
questions.memo: Limiting animal numbers prevents overgrazing — sustainable grazing.

questions.question: Sustainability balances environmental, social and economic needs.
questions.memo: Sustainability balances environmental, social and economic needs together.

questions.question: Using renewable energy like solar power is more sustainable because it:
options: Costs the Earth nothing to ignore
questions.memo: Renewable energy like solar does not run out, making it sustainable.

questions.question: Sustainable use meets today's needs without harming the ____.
questions.memo: Sustainable use protects the future while meeting present needs.

questions.question: Individuals can do nothing to help sustainability.
questions.memo: Individuals can save energy, recycle and choose wisely to help sustainability.

questions.question: Why aim for sustainable resource use?
options: So resources remain for future generations

questions.question: Food security means that people:
options: Have reliable access to enough safe food
questions.expected: Have reliable access to enough safe food
questions.memo: Food security means everyone reliably has enough safe, nutritious food.

options: Change crops, for example to resist pests or grow more

questions.memo: GM crops are altered to improve traits like pest resistance or yield, though it is debated.

questions.memo: Factory farming raises livestock at high density to produce a lot of food.

questions.question: There can be advantages and disadvantages to different ways of producing food.
questions.memo: Each food-production method has trade-offs — economic, environmental, health and ethical.

Use up all the soil quickly

questions.question: Why might people be concerned about factory farming?
